speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime Minister) moved:
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PRECEDENCE OF GOVERNMENT NOTICES OF MOTIONS ON MONDAY, SEPTEMBER 4
speechtext:
That on Monday, September 4, 1950, government notices of motions shall take precedence over the motion for an address to His Excellency the Governor General in reply to his speech at the opening of parliament.
My purpose in presenting this motion now is not to interfere with the debate on the address but to provide an opportunity for calling certain resolutions which are required as a preliminary to the introduction of government bills, so that the recommendation of the crown thereon may be expressed to the house at once. The motions that follow in each case will of course be that the house resolve itself into committee at the next sitting to consider these resolutions.
There seems to be some likelihood that the address will be disposed of in the course of the day. In that event, after disposing of questions and motions for production of papers, it would be the next order of business to have these resolutions considered so that the house may have them before it for its attention.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in view of the Prime Minister's

request, and I believe in view of the general feeling of the house, that this debate should not be too long delayed, I shall endeavour to keep my remarks in the smallest possible compass.
During the last two sessions a good deal of time was spent on the question of Canada being recognized as a nation. Legislation to this end was passed, and there was much discussion of the matter. Excellent speeches were made by hon. members congratulating Canada on becoming a nation. Like many other hon. members, I was glad to find that Canada was a nation. But nationhood implies obligations-obligations	for defence and
obligations to see to it that its commitments to other nations are carried out.
As all hon. members are aware, Canada joined with other nations in the United Nations charter. As I understand it, under the United Nations charter, member nations are not compelled to but are under obligation to come to the assistance of member states in the event of aggression, and indeed to contribute force to resist aggression if aggression has been declared by the security council. This is not a compellable obligation, but it certainly is expected of member states.
There is no question that the government expected there would be trouble in Korea, because in the first sentence of the third paragraph of the booklet "Canada and the Korean Crisis", issued by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson), the following appears:
While this act of open aggression came as a surprise, the existence along the 38th parallel of a situation which constituted a threat to peace was known to the United Nations.
Therefore I ask, should not Canada have been prepared to undertake her obligations under the United Nations charter? What would have been the situation if, instead of Korea being attacked, Norway had been attacked? Norway is one of the members of the Atlantic charter along with Canada. It might very well have been Norway that had been attacked and not Korea. Would Canada have been in a better position to resist aggression in Norway? Indeed, would Canada have been in a position to resist an attack on Canada itself?
The party of which I have the honour to be a member has been termed a war party. That is absolutely untrue. This party is a party of preparedness. It believes that Canada must be prepared to defend itself and to fulfil its obligations to the other members of the free nations of the world.
In the light of the information given by my leader as to the strength of the Russian army, and of the illuminating remarks of
The Address-Mr. Higgins the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Pearkes) and the hon. member for Calgary East (Mr., Harkness) as to Canada's military strength, do hon. members now believe that Canada is in a position to resist an attack on Canada itself?	:
All this information must have been available to the government. What has been done about it? I realize, as do all hon. members,' the limited resources of this country. I realize fully our limited population. But could not better use have been made of the money that was expended by this country for defence purposes? I am not going to labour the question; it speaks for itself, but I will, read to the house an important paragraph from my leader's remarks on September 1, when he said, as reported at page 113 of Hansard:
Let us remember that at no time has this, government been restrained from spending what it has requested for the purposes of defence. No government of Canada has had such a free hand in time of peace to prepare whatever defences are, necessary. No government of Canada has ever spent anything approaching the sum that this' government has spent on defence in years of peace.*
And he concluded that paragraph with' these words:	*
It is the responsibility and duty of every hon/ member to know what has been done and to make sure that we know a great deal more about the. additional expenditures we are being asked to, support than we have been permitted to know in the past.
Well, the only comment I would make- and these are my concluding remarks-will1 be found in the words used recently by a top-' ranking member of the Republican party in the United States:	f
I don't care how many figures the administration produces; the people won't get over it. Something, went haywire somewhere. They had the money. Where are the guns and tanks and planes? That, is what they are asking, and they don't want any' mealy-mouthed answers.	,

One of the most recent speakers said he was of the party of preparedness, and the suggestion is that we are not. The fact is that we are. Look at the record. One of the worthy members of that party has suggested that we wait for conscription. He has suggested that we do not give the boys of our land the privilege of volunteering, which is the greatest privilege given to any man.
I have listened to these experts on war who have attacked our party. Most of them were soldiers, as I was, and some were lawyers, as I am. In those respects they are similar to me, and, like me, they know very little about war. Consequently I feel that in looking at this matter I can look at it as a proven citizen of the Dominion of Canada who fears nothing from them and who can stand on equal ground with any of them.
I have great admiration for the valour and honour of the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Pearkes), but I noticed that occasionally in his speech, as the rest of us do sometimes, he became inconsistent. He said that when the cruisers left Vancouver he felt we were unguarded, because they were a trained force, and in the same breath he said that we should have sent our trained force of military men to Korea. On the one hand the hon. member for Calgary East (Mr. Harkness) said he knew nothing about what was going on in connection with defence expenditures, and in the next breath he said that we are spending unwisely. How could he know what we were doing with defence expenditures if he knew nothing about what was going on? Through the whole thing is a complete pattern of contradiction. I see it as an attack, as an attempt by that party in the opposition to regain ground lost in the debate on railways which preceded this one. They lost there, and by dumb show and noise they are attempting to regain their position-a position which, in the light of history and the record of the Liberal party, can never be regained.
Let us get on with the debate. Let us understand that we are all for Canada and with


Canada. We are here to do a job in an emergency session to carry out a purpose. Let us carry it out faithfully, giving no comfort to the enemy, trusting the cabinet of the elected party of the people to do wisely in the interests of this great country.
Our loyalty is beyond all question. Our faithfulness cannot be questioned, and anyone who slanders the party in power today slanders the vote, the choice and the faith of the Canadian people. Let us do our job as we are intended to do it. Let us do right, as God has taught us to know the right, and Canada will emerge from this crisis as conclusively and as gloriously as she has emerged from other days of tribulation. (Translation):

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the mover of the address in reply (Mr. Cannon) has performed his task with eloquence and skill. In his interesting speech, he said about the railway strike that it was more pressing to settle our own affairs than to restore peace elsewhere. Our first duty is indeed to the citizens of this country.
The charitable dispositions with which our leaders seem to be overflowing lately should first of all be applied to Canada. It is all very well to fulfil our undertakings, but we must show restraint. Let us be cautious and especially avoid being overzealous. The seriousness of the international situation makes it doubly imperative.
At the outset of the Korean crisis the government seemed disposed to adopt a wait-and-see attitude. Then they announced that three destroyers had been put at the disposal of the United Nations; later they sent a few planes to help transport the troops. Finally, in order to satisfy public opinion which had been thwarted and misrepresented by a loud press campaign, a volunteer brigade was formed. Our people are anxiously wondering where this is leading to.
They know only too well that the voluntary system is but the prelude to that dire course called conscription.
Conditions will undoubtedly force the government to impose compulsory service, as the wars of the past have fully shown us.
That is why I believe I can truthfully state that our latest military venture in Korea is opposed not only by large numbers of excellent and worthy citizens, English, French and new Canadians, but also by people practically everywhere in the county I have the honour to represent in this house, as well as in the other ridings of the country. It is the voice of that important body of our population that I want to interpret today.

Patriotism, bravery, courage and altruism are not the exclusive prerogative of the war propagandists and those who listen to them.
I know many young people, fathers and mothers, who would be willing to lay down their lives for the defence of our country. I happen to know many veterans who have already proved themselves capable of heroism and devotion and who would gladly take up arms to repel an invader, but who will not join the United Nations punitive expeditions to the ends of the earth.
Because of air transport, it seems that some of our politicians and newspapermen have lost count of distances and at the same time have lost all sense of patriotism and even all common sense.
Let those who would send us to war, who write or vote accordingly, be the first ones to go. Let them set an example. They might be able by themselves to form another volunteer brigade.
Let no one misconstrue my stand. I am prepared to make every sacrifice for the defence of my country, in order to protect our territorial integrity, to preserve our freedom and to secure a happy life for my fellow citizens, but before sending our youth to graves in distant lands I think I am justified in wondering whether the chance is worth trying and whether the rewards will be worthy of the sacrifice.
By virtue of what protocol, law or agreement is Canada required to assume, in international affairs, more responsibilities than the countries of South America, than India or Turkey?
What are to be the limits to our contribution? Are we to become involved in all conflicts between the followers of the U.S.S.R. and those of the United States? Are we to fight until the last communist has been exterminated from our planet? How long will our foreign policy remain vague, lame and servile?
In a pamphlet entitled "Peace or War", published in 1945 by the information board of Canada, I find the following statement:
In the space of one generation, man has seen two world wars fall upon nations, so that war now has for him tragic implications. Modern inventions, such as the rocket-bomb or the atomic bomb, have upset him and he is horrified at the prospect of a new war which would rend the world and annihilate the human race.
It is not only a question of preserving peace; man must build a world and protect It. There is but one choice:	war or the preservation of
humanity. We have chosen to save the world.
The Address-Mr. Gagnon
It was for that purpose that United Nations representatives assembled at San Francisco and laid the foundations of an international organization aimed at preserving future generations from the scourge of war. To ensure the success of their work they pooled the hopes, efforts and plans of their respective countries and endowed the world with the United Nations charter.
Contained in the provisions of this charter are the principles that govern the various political, economic and social systems in the world of today. In spite of its flaws, it represents the will of nations determined to preserve peace and, above all, it shows ways and means of saving our civilization.
But the charter alone cannot ensure peace for mankind. To achieve its purpose, it must rely on the help and support of all the united nations and human beings that make up these nations. We must all, men and women alike, show our good will and work for the maintenance of peace.
We have the means. Let us make good use of them.
Here are some of them:
To promote mutual understanding rather than misunderstanding.
To seek the factors of unity and cast aside elements of discord.
That was published in 1945:
Saving the world, maintaining peace, these long forgotten ideals.
It is wise to recall, on the verge of a third world war, what the price of the second world war was:
British commonwealth of nations (to May 31, 1945), 434,885 dead or missing and 468,388 wounded; United States (to August 15, 1945), 296,352 dead or missing and 651,168 wounded; U.S.S.R. (to V-E day), from 12 to 15 million dead (civilians and service personnel).
These statistics cover part only of actual casualties.
It is estimated that several years will be needed to give a complete account of the ruins accumulated by war. A few examples will give an idea of the scope of the disaster:
In Greece, from April 1941 to March 1944, 1,085 towns and villages were destroyed. In Great Britain, a third of the houses were damaged or wiped out by bombs. In Holland, at least five years will be needed to redevelop areas submerged by the sea. In Belgium, damage caused to railways alone amounts to more than $50 million. In the U.S.S.R., 71,700 cities and towns were destroyed.
"As for expenses" they have reached almost astronomical figures. In Canada, they amounted to more than $15 billion as of March 31, 1945. It is estimated that with this amount one out of every two Canadian families could have bought an $8,000 house or spent $200 on maintenance and repairs while every family could have bought:

The Address-Mr. Gagnon
The war of 1914 was to be the last one. The leaders, at that time, promised that the war would solve, once and for all, the problems that had disrupted the world and that it would secure lasting peace.
The great slaughter of 1939 was undertaken in the name of freedom, civilization and Christianity, against fascism, Hitlerism and barbarism in order to protect the integrity of the Polish territory. Alas! What fine things we have seen.
When in 1939 Finland was fighting against Russia, for her freedom and survival, the allies, well aware of the heroic past of this small nation, were filled with admiration and Churchill exclaimed: "The service rendered by Finland to humanity is magnificent."
That country had the sympathy of all those who recognize true patriotism and our leaders were anxious to go to her assistance.
When Hitler declared war on Moscow and Russia became our ally, nations that had applauded Finland's glorious feats turned against her because she wanted to remain neutral, after being devastated, battered and vanquished.
She was then considered an enemy of freedom and a traitor to her past. The allies sided with the lion against the slaughtered lamb.
Victory was to witness the triumph of all our prized principles. It was to mean paradise on earth with jobs for all and a home for every soldier. All that had been promised to soldiers in the front line and to civilians on the home front. We know how those illusions and promises turned out.
The Canadian people are still burdened with debts of the last war, and more than ever at grips with inflation which gradually eats up their savings, and with the increasing cost of living which ruins them.
Today we are crusading against communism. We are said to be fighting with guns and munitions a decisive engagement against subversive ideas. On decks of cruisers as well as in the air we are fighting false ideologies. In the name of liberty, civilians are being slaughtered, women and children are being killed in Korea. In the name of liberty we are being reduced to slavery.
What a fiendish and murderous hoax.
We are siding with the South Koreans in their civil war against the North Koreans and the setting up of a communistic regime, while the Franco regime is being refused recognition and support, even though it was and still

is in Spain a stronghold against the servile followers of Moscow and remains in Europe the bulwark of free nations.
We seek to unite our efforts with all those who wage war against communism and at the same time, we neglect one of the best allies we may have on our side, the Vatican,
Here is what The Ensign, on June 17, 1950, wrote in this connection:
(Text):
Frantic efforts are now being made by the statesmen of the still free world to rally in defence against the continuing encroachments of communist persecution. To mobilize arms, to increase Canada's expenditures for military defence, to strain all material efforts of a young country while at the same time refusing to co-operate with other older and experienced nations, engaged in the same task of drawing upon every available moral and spiritual influence, to wit the Vatican, is not a sign of mature judgment. Only when all that is useful is being done can all that is necessary be asked in effort and sacrifice from the people.
(Translation):
The Toronto Telegram, in turn, indicated its point of view in the following terms:
(Text):
There are purely selfish reasons why Canada should follow the example of London and Washington. The Vatican and the Roman Catholic congregation have been one of the great bulwarks against the spread of communism. The Vatican maintains an alert and efficient diplomatic corps. It consequently provides a listening post where a Canadian minister would get vital information relating to international development undiluted and, frequently, in advance of its arrival in other capitals. The "cold war" having reached the stage it has, Ottawa should name a minister without delay. The Roman Catholic church has been a militant leader in the fight against communism. Acknowledging this, it is not difficult to see in the appointment of a Canadian representative to the Vatican an importance beyond the immediate advantage to our foreign service.
(Translation):
Although the frantic and slanted propaganda of the government is attempting to make the people believe the contrary we are not obliged, as members of the United Nations, to supply military forces to repel an aggression, should an aggression occur, which is far from being proved in this case. On the other hand, article 1 of the Atlantic pact states that the signatory nations agree to settle by peaceful means any international conflict in which they may become involved.
(Text):
In an article written by Dorothy Thompson, and published in the Montreal Gazette of September 1, there is the following:
But assuming that there were a United Nations obligation to enforce its own decrees, how, logically, should they be enforced? If they are to be enforced,

as presently provided, only by the voluntary diversion of the armed forces of member states, these forces will be granted or withheld according to the situation of the states involved. Laying aside Mr. Nehru's views on the Asian situation, a government faced with the possibility of war over Kashmir is unlikely to divert substantial forces to Korea; or France, with only five divisions to face the explosive German situation; or Sweden, in imminent danger in the Baltic; or Yugoslavia, walking a tight rope in the Balkans; or Turkey, sitting precariously at the Dardanelles. Russia holds the initiative and, despite abstract idealism, wise government limit their actions to their military capacities, and give priority to home defence.
Thus, if United Nations decrees can be enforced only by the diversion of home and regional forces, these are either withheld or a dozen places weakened in behalf of one-the aggressors picking the one. United Nations decrees could only logically be enforced by a separate police force, responsible to the United Nations, paid out of United Nations budget and composed, like most air forces, entirely, of volunteers, attracted by their allegiance to the United Nations, by high pay and by the conviction that, equipped with the finest modern weapons and kept in a high state of mobility, they would hold the balance on behalf of law and order. The absence of such a force, together with the presence of sanctions whose application is not compulsory, reveals a fundamental United Nations weakness.
The United Nation is a ramshackle organization, without clear definitions and without compulsory sanctions. It cannot enforce anything. It is therefore a more favourable instrument for aggressors, who know exactly its limitations, than for abstract idealists willing to risk their peoples in behalf of a non-existent law of nations. The dreadful thing is that there is no national opposition not tainted by pro-Russian sympathies, or afraid of being so accused if it raises such fundamental questions. There is a sense of being pulled into the unknown by an enemy who leads friends and adversaries alike as puppets on a string while there is no one, of proved patriotism and intellectual and moral power, to. whom the people can turn.
(Translation):
If on the pretext of policing the world for the United Nations we undertake to defend all the countries which are not in a position to oppose Russia victoriously, we shall scatter our forces practically everywhere on the face of the earth and when our own land is directly threatened we shall have no more soldiers or not enough to defend our shores effectively.
A few years ago the Canadian government took orders from Great Britain; today they take them from our neighbours. Thus our external policy is still determined by the leaders of other nations who compel us to imitate their least gesture and to play the part of the frog that wanted to become larger than the bull.
Canada puts herself today in the position of a vassal state awaiting instructions from a power whose authority rests with the United States . . .
These words are taken from Le Soleil, organ of the Liberal party, of June 30 last, which adds:
That syndicate of the United Nations would represent a moral authority if it were really dedicated to the defence of right and justice.
The Address-Mr. Gagnon Unfortunately for the world, the United Nations were never really united in purpose or brotherhood. They are split in two camps whose material interests are incompatible. And that conflict of interests has become irreconcilable because Washington and Moscow can no longer trust each other. A moral authority infinitely higher than that of these two materialistic powers considers them both untrustworthy, even though it dreads more the ungodly aspect of the communist doctrine.
It is under those uncertain conditions that Canada stands ready to take sides in a civil war where Russia takes advantage of the xenophobia of a yellow race to add to the difficulties of the Anglo-American alliance. The immediate cause of that fratricidal conflict is the deliberate mistake which was made by Russia and the United States because they thought it profitable to divide a country once united into two republics separated by a border arbitrarily set to suit the political advantage of their so-called protectors.
In addition to peace considerations and political reasons for which the Canadian people should be induced to refrain from interfering in that intricate matter, there is the risk of a break, in principle, between the nations of the commonwealth. India and Pakistan do not want white people to delay full emancipation of Asia. Even if London overlooks that respectable view, Canada should endeavour to keep on friendly terms with two countries whose liberation from all British domination she once cheered. Should that consideration be disregarded, the peace of mind of all Canadians who want to escape the intrique of foreign politics will be disturbed.
Pandit Nehru, head of a government with socialistic trends, declined to take part in the Korean conflict; that, however, did not prevent him from protecting himself against
70.000	Hindu communists, of whom 3,000 to
4.000	have been jailed. Gandhi's successor summons up all his energy to fight mainly misery and starvation.
Prosperity, indeed, is the foe of communism. As I have stated before in this house, the magic formula that will set up an unyielding bulwark against communism is the abundance of goods and the elimination of poverty.
Employment, housing, fair wages, markets and reasonable prices for farm products, social order and industrial peace strongly established, respect for and compliance with civil and religious laws, triumph of love and order over hatred and anarchy, such, in my opinion, make up the peaceful way the democracies must choose for survival.
Did the last war improve the lot of humanity? Are we happier than we were? No, war has settled nothing and the one now starting, no matter how cruel and prolonged it may be, will bring no better results.
On July 26, in a new encyclical letter, the Pope stated that:
War brings nothing but ruin, death and misery of all sorts.
We are once again asked to uphold democracy and freedom. We must not forget, how-

Controls and orders in council, which plagued us from 1939 to 1945, are standard methods used by dictators to crush the will of free people and turn them into a vast herd of slaves.
The Korean situation has brought about profiteering; the price of essential goods is rapidly increasing, hoarders are happy and so are the munitions manufacturers. Again we have false and artificial prosperity. The harder the war, the more blood will be shed and the more jackals will thrive. Some people must die to guarantee the well-being of others. The government is on the alert. Let us beware; crimes perpetrated in the name of freedom will produce bitter results.
The Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) has indicated that military preparations will cost the Canadian taxpayers hundreds of millions of dollars.
It is surprising that our government can find so easily and so quickly all the money they need for war activities, while it seems to be so difficult for them to find some when they are asked for a more generous pension for the aged, grants essential to the construction of wharfs and public buildings, and relief from taxation.
I wish to recall what the Right Hon. Mackenzie King said in this house on March 30, 1932:
(Text) :
Canada is not a country of unlimited powers: it has not the capacity to stand indefinite strains. We have tremendous tasks to do at home, in housing the people, in caring for the aged and helpless, in relieving drought and unemployment, in building roads, in meeting our heavy burden of debt, in making provisions for Canada's defence and in bringing our standards of living and civilization to the levels our knowledge now makes possible. There is no great margin of realizable wealth for this purpose; we must to a greater or less extent choose between keeping our own house in order, and trying to save Europe and Asia . . .
The decisive test which faces both democracies and dictatorships is the task that faces them at home.
(Translation):
The late Mr. Lapointe, who was then minister of justice, said on the same day:
The time to send expeditionary forces is past.
With these observations, Mr. Speaker, I conclude my remarks.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the outset I wish to repeat some of the things that I said in June of this year in connection with the international situation, so as to make the position I take, and the emphasis I want to make, perfectly clear.


It so happened that when the Korean crisis broke last June both the leader and deputy leader of this group were absent from Ottawa. The leader was in western Canada, and the deputy leader was in Geneva in connection with meetings of the international labour organization. In that situation the members of this group asked me to speak on their behalf so far as it was necessary to state our position here in parliament in connection with the Korean situation. The result was that on three separate occasions during the last week of the last session I made brief remarks concerning this matter.
I do not intend to repeat all that I said at that time, but I should like to read two or three excerpts from the remarks I made on Thursday, June 29, as recorded in Hansard at pages 4385 and 4386. I opened with these words:
Mr. Chairman, following the remarks made yesterday by the Secretary of State for External Affairs I made a very brief statement. However as I look It over In Hansard I realize that within the space of a sentence or two I did express the views which we in this group hold with respect to the present situation. The emphasis I urged yesterday-and I repeat it today

is our complete support of the principles of collective security, and our readiness to carry our support of that principle into all it may involve.
Then followed a paragraph in which I expressed our satisfaction that the security council had met quickly to deal with the situation in Korea, after which I went on to say this:
May I say again that we regard the keeping in repair of the principle and machinery of collective security as the most important task facing us at this time of crisis. If there were a conflict between just two powers, no matter how that conflict came out, it would not guarantee the future peace of the world. Even collective security cannot guarantee peace absolutely, but it has an infinitely better chance than can be achieved by the victory of one power over another.
In the concluding paragraph of that speech I said:
I am sure the Secretary of State for External Affairs is right when he says that the government has the concurrence of all the groups in this house in its readiness to support the action taken, by the United Nations. That is clearly our obligation, and that way alone lies hope. If we can deal with this present crisis on that basis and demonstrate the effectiveness of collective action for peace, we may yet achieve much more in that direction that at times we have dared to hope.
I pointed out earlier in that speech that my support of the principle of collective security was not something new, but that I had made it clear a number of times, particularly in a speech in this house on March 26, 1945. At that time we were discussing the sending of a Canadian delegation to the conference at San Francisco which was to set up the United Nations, and I asserted then that in my view we had to have the kind of international

organization which could enact international law, and that it had to have authority to enforce that law. My support, therefore, of the principle of collective security in this crisis is based on two premises. On the one hand, there is the obvious fact that we must resist and stop aggression, or perish. The other point is that it is extremely important that we should move in the direction of the rule of law in world affairs. For all the faults of the United Nations, and for all the blunders that the United Nations may have made, I feel that we have had, in the collective decision taken by the security council, a move in that direction. I want to add, Mr. Speaker, that that view which I had the privilege of expressing on behalf of this group here in the House of Commons last June has since been endorsed and confirmed by our party at a national convention which was held in the city of Vancouver in July of this year.
I have taken these few minutes, sir, to spell out that position in order to make it crystal clear that we in this movement know precisely where we stand when aggression is committed. It must be resisted; it must be stopped. We know where we stand with regard to the rule of law in international affairs. But we also take the position-and this is the point on which I wish to lay emphasis-that unless we accompany the military action that we are prepared to support in order to resist aggression with other measures such as those which have been suggested time and again by the Secretary of State for External Affairs, measures which we have called for down through the years, I submit that the money we shall spend and the lives that will be lost, sad to say, will be in the position of having "gone down the drain". Unless we accompany our military action with a positive effort to develop underdeveloped countries and to persuade the people, particularly those in Asia as well as those in other parts of the world, that we in the democratic world really have something better than what is being proclaimed to them from the other side, we can win the war so far as military action is concerned, but we can lose the whole struggle in which we are engaged for a better and a more secure world for humankind.
I know that emphasis is placed on this point not only 'by those of us in this group but by others. One hears it in radio speeches every week. One reads it in newspaper and magazine articles by a great many people; and as I have already indicated, one hears it in this House of Commons, as well as outside of parliament, from the Secretary of State for External Affairs. But what is this country doing about it other than applauding the fine statements that the Secretary of State for External Affairs has made? We have before us now, on the order paper, measures 60269-14J
The Address-Mr. Knowles which the government proposes to take to meet this aggression. But in those measures I see nothing that supports the strong statements that the Secretary of State for External Affairs has made when he agrees with us that military action is necessary-let there be no doubt about that-but that military action alone is not enough.
Let me put on the record again-because I agree with them, and because I feel they should be backed up with action, with measures, with money voted by this house- some of the things which the Secretary of State for External Affairs has said. I quote from page 90 of Hansard of August 31:
These other weapons,-
He is talking about the weapons of the communists.
-or many of them, are insidious and hard to counter. Often they work underground and in the dark; indeed sometimes they work best when they are driven underground. They can be met and overcome, as indeed they are being overcome, by the initiative of the free world in many places, notably in western Europe; but they cannot be defeated by military action alone. Military strength is absolutely necessary, of course, but it must be supplemented by imaginative economic and social programs if the march of communism as a social and economic doctrine is to be halted before it reaches a point at which a military attack will commend itself to the members of the politburo as likely to succeed.
I applauded that statement when the minister made it, andi I applaud it again. But where are these imaginative economic and social programs which he admits must accompany 'military action if we are to halt the spread' of communism? He said later-and I quote from page 91 of Hansard:
We in the west, while laying bare the trickery and malice of soviet protestations, must at the same time provide some real satisfaction for those everlasting hungers for bread, security and freedom to which the communists pretend to cater. Otherwise we shall not secure the support of those in many parts of the world, and particularly in Asia, on whose co-operation we must rely in the days ahead.
I fully agree, Mr. Speaker. But we now have 'before us proposals asking for what amounts to nearly a billion dollars. None of it is for economic development or for economic aid to underdeveloped countries. None of it backs up the minister's own contention that we must, at this time, accompany necessary military action with these other measures. I realize that, after previous wars, particularly the two in our time, we have said that the next time we will do it better, if there has to be a next time. But always when the next time comes we say that once this immediate task, the military problem, is over, then we will get down to these economic and social matters. The minister is perfectly right. It is not a case of getting around to these economic and
a04	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Knowles social objectives after the military action is over. The economic and social objectives must accompany military action or it may be too late after it is all over. Now is the time that we have got to convince both the people whose cause we are defending iti Asia and other parts of the world-and our own people-that our idea with regard to economic and social organization is really and unquestionably the better one, as I believe it to be, even with all the improvements we need here at home.
We have all been disturbed by the vague answers to questions as to objectives, in Korea and in Asia, that have been put to those in high places. The answers of various military leaders have shown a lack of appreciation of what was meant. There is real point, I submit, in statements that have been made by some of our church leaders. For example, I think of the questions being asked in a current issue of the United Church Observer as to the aims of our fighting in Korea. There seems to be a tendency on the part of the government to feel that because a war is being fought, other questions should be held over until later. The (Secretary of State for External Affairs knows *-he has said it clearly-that that is not so. He said it when there was no conflict and he was able to speak academically, but he has said it now in the midst of a serious conflict- that unless we accompany necessary military action with these other measures we can lose the very struggle in which we are engaged, namely, the struggle for a free world in which people can satisfy their everlasting desire for peace and bread and freedom. I agree, but let us do something about it.
The Secretary of State for External Affairs said again on page 96:
Furthermore, just as we have learned slowly and painfully the dangers of great economic gulfs betweens various sections of our own country, now we must begin to learn the parallel lesson that it is dangerous to let such gulfs exist between various countries without doing anything to try to narrow them.
Please note: this is not a statement made by the Secretary of State for External Affairs in a time of peace when he could utter words as in a vacuum; this is a statement made in this house on August 31, when men are dying on the battlefront in Korea. And I quite agree with the position he takes. He continues:
That effort must be spread over many generations; but a start should be made, and now a start is being made.
I dared to hope from that little sentence- his words that a start is now being made- that when the government's measures in


relation to the international situation reached the order paper there would be in them at least some measure of economic aid for underdeveloped countries. But no; it is not there- not a nickel. I go on with the quotation:
For just as it is impossible to have a healthy society in any one country if some individuals are living below the level of subsistence, so it is impossible to have a healthy world society when whole nations are subject to starvation and disease. Throughout large areas of Asia, such conditions now exist. Where they exist, they are natural breeding grounds for communism. These malarial swamps of poverty must somehow be drained off if we are ever to see stability and freedom in the new Asian countries. And if we do not see stability and freedom there, we may find difficulty in maintaining them in other parts of the world.
The whole burden of my speech is that I agree one hundred per cent with the statements that the Secretary of State for External Affairs has made, but I am looking for something on the order paper to back up his contention that the time to bring forward these other measures, other than the necessary military action, is not after the war is over, but now; for it is right now that we need the allegiance and the support not only of our own people in this country but of millions of people in Asia and in other parts of the world who cannot but be bewildered as to what it is all about.
I point out, Mr. Speaker, that we like to call this action in which we are engaged a police action. We have not declared war. I quite agree that that is what collective security is, but I submit that if we use that parallel we should remember that in domestic society police action is not the only way in which we deal with crime. We seek to rehabilitate criminals. We impose sentence, of course. But we also spend a great deal of time and effort in trying to remove the conditions that lead to crime. I need not go into that now, because we are familiar with the things that we are seeking to do. I submit that that should be the picture so far as the international situation is concerned.
I do not want to detract by one iota from what is being done in the military sense. I have said that. I have said very clearly that so far as I am concerned, so far as this group is concerned and so far as our movement is concerned, we back the necessity of military action to resist aggression, (a) because aggression has to be stopped or we perish; and (b) because it is the result of a decision of the security council, which is the nearest thing to the rule of law that we have had in international affairs up to the present time.
I have before me a copy of an interesting speech made by the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Fournier) when he was representing Canada at the eleventh session of the economic

and social council in Geneva. The speech was made on July 11 of this year. I read it with great interest; but I must point out that though the subject under discussion was aid to underdeveloped countries, about all we get in the speech is agreement with the idea and support of the proposal that the matter deserves intensive study; there is nothing before us now to accompany necessary military action with these other proposals. It is the same old story-fine words but nothing to back them up.
As I have listened to the debate in this house I cannot take issue with the concern of those who have discussed the military aspects of the present situation. One cannot gainsay the terrible and ghastly prospect that faces us if we do not take police action, military action, if you will, to stop aggression. But we have done that before. We have done it twice in the lifetime of most of us in this place, and we cannot but wonder where it will lead us unless-this time-we add something new. That is my point, Mr. Speaker. That is the point the Secretary of State for External Affairs made. Military action, yes; but we must add something new, and that something new is an attempt to persuade the people, particularly of Asia, that our way offers them something substantial; and we could do that in various ways, particularly by economic aid to these underdeveloped countries. This special session of parliament-not next year, not when the war is over, but this special session of parliament-should be taking a lead from the Secretary of State for External Affairs, and should right now be appropriating money to assist in a program of economic aid to those underdeveloped countries. I think there are other things that should be done. The other day one of my colleagues suggested the matter of bringing students from other countries to our country to learn our ways, to learn our industrial methods, our farming methods, our ways of organizing trade unions, and our whole democratic approach.
In addition, Mr. Speaker, we must consider the whole question of the support of our own people, which is extremely important. One of the ways to do that is again to follow what the Secretary of State for External Affairs said in his speech the other day. I like the figure of speech that he used toward the end of his address when he said this:
This effort will interfere with our comfortable peacetime existence. It is not going to be something that will break the camel's back, because the Canadian camel's back is pretty wide.
I agree, but I also agree with his next sentence:
But it will be something that may require a readjustment of the load already on that back,-
The Address-Mr. Knowles
I should not fail to read the whole sentened. It continues:	f
-and will also add to that load.
I agree with him that it would not breajc the Canadian camel's back. I agree with him that that load will add something to the load already there, but I also agree with him in the part of that sentence that I want to underline, namely, his insistence that the increased load may require a readjustment of the load already on the camel's back.
That means, Mr. Speaker, that this session of parliament has to do something about rising prices. We are not doing that if no action is taken to prevent prices from running wild. I was interested in' the letter which was sent to the government-perhaps directly to the Prime Minister-the other day by the Canadian association of consumers, in which they called for measures to prevent rising prices. In that letter-I do not have it before me-as I recall it, there was something to this effect, that the Canadian association of consumers was gratified that parliament was being called together at this time to deal with all of the various economic problems that were thrown into the picture by virtue of the international situation. Well, one of the most serious problems that has been thrown into the picture is this problem of rising prices. So far the only government suggestion for dealing with this problem is additional control in the hands of the Minister of Trade and Commerce regarding basic materials, and perhaps something by way of increased taxes, leaving prices themselves to go up or down as they may according to economic conditions. The chance of prices doing anything else but go up under the proposals or the lack of proposals that we have now is unanswerable. According to the last report of the bureau of statistics, issued at the end of last week, the cost of living index is now at its highest level in bur history- 168-5. And, as a comment on that, the bureau of statistics says that the food index has reached an all-time high of 216-7.
A great deal is being said these days in support of the economic theory that advocates the necessity of draining off purchasing power to prevent inflation, but, sir, the housewives in my constituency cannot understand that kind of talk at all. They do not understand the process of draining off their purchasing power when they have not enough now to buy the food they require for their families at these prices which have reached a high point of 216-7.
Like other members in the house I try to be a good husband when I am home and do some of the shopping. I am amazed,

The Address-Mr. Knowles as I am sure other members must be, at the prices of goods offered in our food stores. My heart really goes out in sympathy many times to housewives who stand at meat -counters or look over the groceries on store shelves and try to figure out how they can buy the cheaper cuts and the cheaper foods so as to get by with the limited purchasing power they possess.
I agree with the Secretary of State for External Affairs. The only trouble is that he should be over here lecturing to the cabinet, instead of putting up a front of words for the government. He is right-there should be a redistribution of the load on the camel's back. One of the ways in which we can distribute that load is for the government to bring in at this session a measure which would make possible the control of prices, so that, instead of going on up from this very high figure of 168-5 for all -commodities and 216-7 for food, there might be some sort of roll-back; people would then have a chance to keep going in this time of crisis, and they would be convinced that our democratic way is really the better way.
I know our people, as do all members in the house. They will back the government, they will back their country and they will back the United Nations in an effort to resist aggression, even though prices do run wild. They will do it with courage and sacrifice, even if they are let dow-n; because they realize that, even with all its faults, our democratic way is better than the totalitarian way. But they would do it with a great deal more spirit and with much greater confidence if this time steps were taken, not after the war is over but while it is on, to establish security and justice and real freedom here at home.
We all remember well the words of Mr. King during the early stages of world war II, that if we were to wait until after the war was over to look for the beginnings or the foundations of a new society we would look in vain. It had to be started then. All right; I am with the Secretary of State for External Affairs one hundred per cent in his insistence that the load on the camel's back should be redistributed now, and not after the war is over, so that the Canadian camel can carry the load. One of the ways to do it is to take action at this session on this staggering question of runaway prices.
Similarly I support with all the vigour I can the insistence of the leader of this group, the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell), upon an early implementation of the report of last session's special committee on old age security. I have been annoyed at the number of newspaper editors


across the country who are now suggesting that because of the increased costs of defence that program will have to be put on the shelf. I am glad to note, however, that as yet there has not been any announcement of that kind that could be attributed to a government source. So far it has just been found in editorials in newspapers such as the Winnipeg Free Press. In my view, that position is entirely wrong. In my view, now in the time to implement that report.
I submit our people are perfectly sound when they say that if money can be found for increased defence costs, and if it can be found for military assistance to other parties in the North Atlantic pact, it can also be found for economic aid to underdeveloped countries, and for an objective such as the social security program embodied in the bluebook that committee brought down at the end of the last session.
I well remember that in that committee some members said they were staggered by the amount of money involved in the various programs submitted. However, I do submit that those who were members of the committee will feel now that those amounts were not so staggering, to put it mildly, when compared with the sums of money we are called upon to vote at this session, and the sums of money that the present international situation, as it is developing, may yet cost.
I submit again that even if the government lets the people of Canada down and does not arrange for the implementation of that report, those people will support resistance to aggression; there is no doubt about it. But they will support it with much greater spirit, and much greater confidence -that there is a future ahead for our democratic way of life, if this time something new is added; if this time we take steps to redistribute the load over the camel's back, and if this time we take steps toward a new society while military action is going on.
I would emphasize one other point. It seems to me of extreme importance that we keep in the best state of repair our whole democratic and parliamentary processes. We hav^ before us a number of measures to be discussed later in the session, perhaps today or tomorrow, which, to say the least, ask parliament to give pretty wide powers to the cabinet. I think because of the situation a case will and no doubt can be made for increased power. But I submit that we must not allow expediency to run away with basic and fundamental principles. We must remember that the strength of political democracy as we know it lies in the parliamentary system.

Somehow the people back home look upon parliament as consisting of the ordinary backbenchers of all parties in the House of Commons. When parliament meets and makes decisions, even though the people may not like the decisions the majority makes, they are somewhat more palatable to them than when they are made by the cabinet, oil by itself, exercising power by order in council. For that reason I submit the government should think carefully about any program involving extreme powers placed in the hands of the cabinet, without the necessity of having parliament here or calling it back from time to time. This is no time to whittle away at the processes of democracy. This is no time to abrogate the rights .of parliament, to which the government is responsible. That must not be forgotten. This is a time when we are trying to tell the whole world that the democratic and parliamentary way is the better way. Let us keep that way in the best possible state of repair.
At the risk of repetition let me sum up what I have been saying by making my position as clear as I can make it. Right from the beginning of the Korean crisis we have supported the principle of collective security. We urged Canada to get in behind the United Nations, and we have supported the steps Canada has taken in support of what the United Nations has asked. That support is consistent with our prior position that, so far as we are concerned, collective security and the rule of law in world affairs are absolutely necessary. Those of us in this group have supported that position clearly. We have supported it in the House of Commons, and it was supported at our convention held since the last sitting of the house.
We believe aggression has to be resisted; but we believe firmly, with the Secretary of State for External Affairs that, this time, in resisting aggression, something new must be added to the necessary military measures, and that "something new", includes at least economic assistance to underdeveloped countries, ways and means of convincing the people of Asia and other parts of the world that we have something better; and it must include also a determined effort on the home front to convince our people of the superiority of our way.
I have already suggested ways in which that home-front job can be done. Our suggestion is to do something about runaway prices, to do something about social security, and to make sure that we keep our democratic and parliamentary processes in the best possible state of repair during this
The Address-Mr. Knowles critical time in the history of our nation and in the history of the world.
This is indeed a critical time; but if we will take a lead from what has been said by the Secretary of State for External Affairs; if the government will put his proposals in concrete form on the order paper, I am convinced that we can yet have that brighter future for our country and for the people of the world which all of us dare to believe to be our destiny.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I know it is a custom that has become stale with repetition, but in the light of circumstances I extend my congratulations to the mover (Mr. Cannon) and the seconder (Mr. Bennett) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. Both are young men, and without the benefit of young minds parliament cannot discharge its responsibilities and assume its prerogatives.
I listened with intense interest to the hon. member for Ontario (Mr. Thomson), who gave the house quite a lecture on constitutional matters and the functions of the opposition. It was a clear speech, but it revealed an attitude which in my opinion is a negation of democratic principles. The hon. member surprised me when he said that he regards cabinets with such high approval. He said, "Trust the cabinet". I understand that it will not be very long before he becomes the leader of the opposition in the Ontario house. If he does, his ideas with regard to government will have to undergo a tremendous
208	.	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Diefenbaker change. The attitude that an opposition is something to put up with on occasion is prevalent in some quarters. As I listened to the hon. member I was reminded of a summary of the power of the House of Commons made by Jennings in his monumental work, "Parliament", and I should like to repeat it because it epitomizes my concept of parliament. I quote:
It holds its position partly because of its great traditions. It has fought kings and dismissed them. It has raised up an army to destroy a king and was itself destroyed by its army; only to recall another king and to rise up again on the site of its own destruction. It has been modified and reformed to meet the changes of centuries. It has been led by the greatest men that the country has produced-Pitt the elder and Pitt the younger, Sir Robert Peel, Disraeli and Gladstone, Lloyd George; it has seen the greatest wits and orators in opposition to each other; it has, above all, achieved the pinnacle of freedom by listening to men like Charles James Fox, Sir Henry Campbell-Bannerman, Lloyd George and Mr. Ramsay MacDonald and Churchill who dared to be unpopular and, in the cant phrase, "unpatriotic", because they insisted on speaking the truth as they understood it.
That is what parliament is for. If the cabinet is to be trusted; if we are to accept at face value what ministers say, then we had better all be absent from this house. We would need no parliament. The hall-mark of democracy is not political uniformity; the hall-mark of democracy is parliament operating, as the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) said the other day, as it did last week, when, regardless of differences, parliament spoke with power and decision. Its speedy action did more to restore parliament in the public mind than anything else that has happened in recent years.
I know that cabinets long in power tend to believe that they rule by divine right;
I know that they do not welcome oppositions, but a one-party state is not a democratic state. It is only when there is a vigilant opposition, prepared to take the stand that it believes necessary for the preservation of freedom, that there can be freedom.
We have met here on a serious occasion. Unless what the hon. member for Ontario has said is in fact indicative of the attitude of the government, I find it difficult to understand why the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent)
>
seems so anxious to get rid of parliament at this time. I find it difficult to understand why he seemed so anxious the other day to do that which was not done in 1939, when one whom the government has always called a master parliamentarian, now deceased and honoured as part of the heritage of our country, realized that an opposition could work only if parliament were allowed to meet at reasonable hours. The regular rules and routine have been denied to us. In this respect the Prime Minister did not give


evidence of that co-operation and that recognition of the needs of the opposition that is so necessary in our parliamentary system.
Korea has dramatized the need of action if freedom is to be preserved. Canadians do not need proof that communism has become an outlaw internationally. They know what communism has done. The Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson), in language of powerful imagery, showed what communism had done in the dethroning of human personality, the destruction of liberty and the prostitution of men everywhere to its treasonable designs.
I agree with the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), that the time has come when in addition to material defence measures this nation must draw from spiritual springs, and there must be on the part of each of us an active determination to see to it that freedom is preserved.
Communism has struck in Korea. It may strike in other parts of the world-in Turkey, Greece, west Germany or Indo-China. Wherever there are puppet states there is danger; there are potential Koreas.
Parliament has an opportunity now to be the epitome of the nation's will; to act, and to act with power and accelerated activity. The hon. member for Ontario says, "Tryst the cabinet". Unacquainted as I am with matters of national defence, I have been of the opinion on more than one occasion in the last two years that some of the criticisms that were being made might have gone too far. I could not believe that a government would contend, as this government said so often, that all was well, that Canada was prepared, if such were not the case. My hon. friend says, "Trust the cabinet".

The decision of the United Nations to act against aggression is a long step forward toward the dream of mankind since the days of Grotius that there should in fact be some system of punishment internationally for wrongdoing on the part of nations.
The concept of an international police force goes back to the time of Castlereagh, when he advanced that proposition before the congress of Vienna in 1815. The statesman who took a stand against it then was Alexander I of Russia. I was in San Francisco in a very humble capacity in 1945. I saw there the building of what I thought would be a new world. Now, sir, may I presume to make a suggestion in connection with the United Nations. It has the power to declare what proceedings should be taken against aggressors, after declaring that aggression has taken place. Action requires a two-thirds vote. Ten days is too long in a world of uncertainty, and I submit that the necessary change should be made in procedure, in view of the fact that the security council is emasculated by the presence of the U.S.S.R. The July issue of the United Nations World refers to the hidden resources this country possesses', resources necessary to the development and expansion of an all-out

Next, what is being done about the matter of civil defence? I attended the national mayors' conference in Saskatoon. They discussed the problem and agreed on the necessity of something being done. A committee has been set up as between the dominion, the provinces and the municipalities. The ultimate administration will rest with the municipalities. In the establishment of necessary defence measures for this country I suggest that consideration be given to the financing of civil defence-which after all is a segment of our national defence-by the dominion as a whole.
Finally, sir, in connection with the mobilization of the reserve army the hon. member for Greenwood placed certain suggestions before the house on Saturday. A complaint among those in the reserve army is the fact that when they give their time and their energies to this form of service they are subject to income tax. They should be relieved of such taxes, thus encouraging them and showing them that we recognize the service they are giving voluntarily.
Canadians want more than verbal assurances. They want more than rhetoric in respect to a period which is one of the most dangerous in our history. They want this government and this parliament to give them- absolute assurance that what we do will preserve freedom to the limit of our capacity; that parliament will be dynamic; that the action taken will be such as to create the high morale that comes when people join together in the realization that everything is being done that can be done to meet the challenge confronting the country.
The people are fearful today; for, with Korea in their minds, they ask themselves: What about the optimistic statements of the last few years? For these the government must be held strictly to account. We in the opposition, and private members in all parts

of the house, cannot do the things that Canada demands. But what we can do is to demand that the government act, so that when the session is over we shall, in a spirit of unity, realize that if austerity once more has come to this nation, it is necessary for our survival, and be able to assure the people of Canada of the need of personal sacrifice, as we were able to do during the days of war. What we want to be able to do is to assure this nation and to assure the United Nations that we shall do more than make optimistic statements; that the maintenance of collective security requires more than attendance at conferences where great and abiding principles are enunciated but too often forgotten when the delegates return.
This is what Churchill said:
Man in this moment of his history has emerged in greater supremacy over the forces of nature than has ever been dreamed of before. He has it in his power to solve quite easily the problems of material existence. He has conquered the wild beasts, and he has even conquered the insects and the microbes. There lies before him, if he wishes, a golden age of peace and progress. All is in his hand. He has only to conquer his last and worst enemy-himself. With vision, faith and courage, it may still be within our power to win a crowning victory for all.
My hope and my prayer is that we shall accept the responsibility at this time of assuring the Canadian people that wherever there is aggression it will be met, and of assuring the United Nations that we view our responsibilities as more than words in an idealistic charter, and that we in parliament will act now.
