Mr. Speaker, the speech from the throne at this special session contains two short paragraphs, one referring to the railway strike and the other to the situation which has

arisen because of aggression in South Korea. In effect we are now dealing with that second paragraph, which reads:
You will also be asked to give urgent consideration to the measures for increased national security and international co-operation required by the fighting in Korea and the increasingly grave international situation which that struggle reflects. That was the original reason for summoning you to this special session.
To that paragraph we of the official opposition have moved an amendment, which I propose to support, and which reads as follows:
That the following words be added to the address:
"We regret that Your Excellency's advisers have failed to provide adequately for the defence of Canada and have failed to take steps to deal with inflation and the rapidly rising cost of living."
At the outset may I say it is perfectly clear that the people of the world, including Canadians, are living in a new era which may well be called the Korean era. I believe it would be wise for the members of this house to give some thought to developments we may expect in this new era which we entered so suddenly during the last week end in June.
In the first place, we may expect open aggression at any time by Russia or her satellites. In Korea the communists challenged the United Nations, the United States and all the democracies, including Canada. Probably they thought that challenge would be ignored, but instead our great neighbour the United States took it up at once. For such courageous action she deserves the gratitude of every person in all the democratic countries of the world. Because Russia was sulking and was not sitting in at the meetings of the security council the United Nations were able to act. That fact gives me great encouragement. It shows that all the stupid people are not on our side. We think that we are the only ones who make mistakes but here we have these communists, whom we sometimes think have all the brains in the world, making the great mistake of staying away from the security council meetings, pouting, and thereby giving the democracies a chance to take action through the United Nations.
No attack will be initiated by a democratic country; everyone in this chamber today knows that. If there is an attack it will be started by the communists, and will be started without warning. There will be little or no time for us or any other nation on our side to make further preparations. In other words, in this new era Canadians must not be startled by an attack. Then we must expect to find Russia and her satellites stronger than we thought they were, and the democracies weaker, particularly in ground forces. I believe that the democracies have been
The Address-Mr. Green paying too much attention to machines of war. They have been sitting back thinking that if they have the most modern equipment, if they have plenty of atom bombs, then there is no fear of war, or if war should start that they would always be able to win without very much effort. It comes back to the old story of the first great war which you and I, Mr. Speaker, know so well, the old story of the p.b.i. There always has to be somebody brave enough to go right in and root out the enemy. I hope the democracies will remember that in these grim days.
We can expect no real peace for a long time, perhaps not in the lifetime of any member in this chamber today. Certainly there will be no real peace in the lifetime of the present parliament. It is clear that in the lifetime of this parliament there will be either a third world war or an armed peace with war prevented only because we are so strong that the communists dare not fight. It is clear too that in this new era we must be ready to defend ourselves at a moment's notice, and that we must stand beside-I repeat, beside and not behind-our friends. The penalty for failure to do so is death or slavery for the people of the democracies and the end of Christian civilization.
We are gathered together in this special session as representatives of the Canadian people to consider the course that Canada should follow in this Korean era. I think our duty was put very clearly in an editorial in the Vancouver Province a week ago today, which contained this sentence:
There are tough, urgent problems facing Canada, and they can be solved only by straight thinking and plain speaking.
Today I have a few thoughts that I wish to place before the house, but more particularly before the ministry, because the nation must look for leadership to the members of the present cabinet. The first thought is that they should tell the people the whole truth, even though it may be unpleasant. Let the cabinet remember Churchill's famous speech in 1940, when he reminded the British people that they need expect nothing but blood, sweat and tears. Let the Canadian cabinet, from the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) down, tell the people the truth. Last Friday the Prime Minister made a statement in the house that did not come up to those requirements. I believe he was carried away by the exuberance of the moment when he said that the crisis would last for only ten months. Mind you, in his speech there were qualifications, but here is the heading in an Ottawa paper:
Ten months of crisis seen by P.M. but looks for dawn of era of lasting peace.
216	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Green
The first paragraph of the newspaper story reads:
The next ten months are crisis months, Prime Minister St. Laurent told the House of Commons yesterday, but he hoped and felt that "we may not be far from the dawn of an era of lasting peace."
Similar articles appeared in all other Canadian newspapers which I have had an opportunity of reading since that time. Such statements are misleading; they are merely wishful thinking in these times. There is nothing temporary about our danger. It will not be over in ten months. We shall be mighty lucky if it is over in ten years. If the Prime Minister really believes the statement he made, then it is time that Canada had a new Prime Minister.
Then there was the speech of the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) last week. Its general tone was: Everything will be all right; why are you worrying?-trust me and all will be well. His attitude throughout this crisis has been such that I believe the Canadian people may very well question his fitness to be Minister of National Defence. He must be far more realistic in the leadership he gives to the Canadian people. What Canada needs more than anything else today is the Churchill touch in her leaders, and very little of that is visible thus far.
The original reason for calling the special session was to deal with the question of sending ground forces to Korea. It took the government a long time to make up its mind. The regular session for this year should not have been prorogued; in any event we should have been called back weeks ago; yet until the railway strike occurred, the intention was that we would not be called for a further six weeks or two months. However, here we are, and I presume the government wants to know where everybody stands on the question of sending ground forces to Korea. Personally I approve that course. For years it has been Canadian policy to keep war away from our shores. My deskmate, the hon. member for Lake Centre <Mr. Diefenbaker), quoted a statement to that effect by the Minister of National Defence, which appeared in the United Nations World for the month of July. The Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) made a similar statement on August 31 when in the course of his speech he said that Canada's defence policy was designed to be capable of rapid expansion in the event of a general war which might require Canada to be defended outside of Canada. I can never understand how any Canadian who knows anything about war can be against a policy IMr. Green.]

the aim of which is to keep the fighting in somebody's else country. Surely that is just plain common sense.
Then we had a clear-cut obligation to the United Nations to send forces to Korea. It is only there that aggression can be fought at this time. Perhaps the only way a third world war can be prevented is through successful fighting by the United Nations in Korea.
Although I approve the sending of ground forces, I regret more than I can say the hesitation and evasion which have been shown by this government along the tortuous course by which it finally reached the decision that Canada should send ground troops. I have here a revealing publication issued by the Secretary of State for External Affairs entitled "Canada and the Korean Crisis." It tells the whole story. On June 27 the security council, acting with promptitude, passed a resolution, the last paragraph of which reads as follows:
Recommends that the members of the United Nations furnish such assistance to the republic of Korea as may be necessary to repel the armed attack and to restore international peace and security in the area.
On July 14 there was a direct request from the Secretary General of the United Nations to Canada, along with the other nations who were members of that organization, in which we find this:
-there is an urgent need for additional effective assistance. I should be grateful, therefore, if your government would examine its capacity to provide an increased volume of combat forces, particularly ground forces.
On July 19 we had a statement from the Prime Minister. He did not face that request for ground forces. Oh, no; he evaded that request in his speech to the Canadian people. He said that we would recruit our active forces, and we would send air transport to help carry United States soldiers to the battlefield, but there was not one word about Canada sending ground troops promptly as requested by the United Nations. We find that on July 21 Canada sent a note to the Secretary General of the United Nations. In that note there appears this strange paragraph:
You will observe that in Mr. St. Laurent's statement-
A copy of the Prime Minister's statement was sent as well.
-reference is made to the Canadian government's willingness to give consideration to participation in a United Nations force for service in Korea should a decision to that effect be taken by the security council.
Although the security council had passed a resolution on June 27, almost a month before this particular note.

After a further three weeks the Prime Minister, in a broadcast to the people of Canada, announced that the government would send ground forces to Korea. There was no announcement that it would send one of our active army battalions, which was certainly better trained than any group could be which would have to be enlisted from the cities, towns and villages of Canada. The announcement was not made that we would send one battalion of troops quickly when time was of such importance. No; we were going to raise a Canadian army special force which would be ready to fight in six months or more. From the statements made by the ministry it appears that that force will not be in a position to fight for at least six months.
In today's press there appears an article headed: "Pleads for men: MacArthur wants more troops fast". The article reads:
My gravest concern is for a prompt build-up of the now outnumbered ground forces of this command . . .
I still feel it my duty to report to you that contributions must be forthcoming without delay if this threat to international security is to be resolved promptly.
Today the news on the radio tells us that our friends have been driven back several more miles. Canadian government policy, in effect, amounted to this: Let somebody else do the fighting for the first six months or a year. It would have been just the same if the aggression had been against a member of the North Atlantic pact. If there was no force to send to Korea; then there was none to send to help one of these North Atlantic treaty nations if it had been attacked. Yet Canada was the first nation to sign the North Atlantic treaty. I recall that the government took a lot of credit for that fact. How the ministry rushed that approval through this house in their desire for Canada to be the first nation to sign the treaty! I repeat that I regret this hesitation and evasion on the part of the government. It is not in line with the courage of the Canadian people, and it is particularly unfortunate in view of our relationship with our neighbour, the United States.
Then, Mr. Speaker, I urge that Canadians serve with a British commonwealth division, and that the government announce such a policy before the end of this special session. Here again we have hesitation and evasion. The Australians and the British have troops in the Far East. Britain has troops either already in action or going into action in Korea within a few hours. Australia has had troops in the army of occupation in Japan. There is a British commonwealth
The Address-Mr. Green base for troops in Japan to which Canadian troops could go, and yet we find Canada hanging back.
I propose to read a few extracts from press dispatches, the first of which is dated July 28, before Canada decided to send any ground forces. The first two paragraphs read as follows:
The Australian government formally and fully informed the Canadian government of its proposal that a commonwealth division should be formed for the fighting in Korea, before any announcement was made in the press, it was learned here today.
The plan envisaged other commonwealth troops taking part along with those of Australia and New Zealand, but no direct request was made to Canada to participate, though obviously the Australians, like the Americans, would have been happy if Canadians did join the ground forces in Korean fighting.
On August 10 there was a press dispatch from Ottawa to the effect that the government was going to let parliament decide with what troops the Canadians would fight. A few days later an editorial appeared in the Vancouver Sun, which paper is a supporter of this government. In this editorial I believe the Sun represents the thinking of every person in the province of British Columbia. It is headed "A Commonwealth Division", and reads in part as follows:
And there is no valid reason why it should not approve its grouping with other commonwealth units as part of a commonwealth division. To the majority of Canadians, surely, this would seem a natural thing.
Supposing it goes to Korea, how would the special brigade fight? As an independent unit? Hardly. It would be grouped with other units into a division. If it is to be a composite division, what better arrangement could be made than one of all-commonwealth character?
There is one reason above all why, since we are not sending more than a brigade, it should be grouped with the brigades that will be going from Australia and Britain and the artillery from New Zealand. And that is that these are all commonwealth units and we are all proud to belong to the commonwealth.
Yet the Minister of National Defence speaking here last week, when I asked him whether our brigade was to be in a commonwealth division, hummed and hawed. He said that the brigade will have British-type equipment; that there will be other commonwealth units and they too will have British-type equipment; that perhaps it might serve with them and perhaps it might not; but he thought we had better leave that decision to the United Nations command. If any hon. members would care to read his statement, they will find it at pages 99 and 100 of Hansard.
I believe that the Minister of National Defence hopes that the Canadian brigade will serve either with United States forces or with a United Nations division in which our
218	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Green men would have as associates troops from other nations such as Turkey, Thailand-and I mean no discredit to them-and other nations which have volunteered to send troops to the Korean fight.
The government appears to be completely ignoring tradition and history. Thirty-two years ago some of us fought in the battle of Amiens, on August 8, 1918. Beside the second Canadian division fought Australian troops and you could have no finer troops on your flank. As to New Zealanders, I do not need to remind any veteran in this house what Canadian troops thought of them. I need only quote from a book on Field Marshal Rommel by Desmond Young, which has recently been published. There we find what that great fighting leader thought of New Zealanders. In this book I find this statement:
For New Zealanders, individually and collectively, he had almost an affection.
That was the feeling of the great German commander toward our blood brothers in New Zealand. As to the British guards brigade, there have been no finer troops in the modem world; or the Highland regiments, with all their dash and all their gallantry. It is just too bad that in this Canadian army special force there is no Highland regiment; there should be one to represent the Scotsmen of this nation.
Does the government forget that ten years ago the British commonwealth was standing alone against the enemy; that for a whole year, with the exception of the help of gallant little Greece, the British commonwealth stood alone and saved civilization? Yet here we have a Minister of National Defence who is afraid or unwilling to announce that Canadian troops are going to serve with the British commonwealth division.
One of the greatest tragedies of our time is that the British commonwealth is not today a third great world power standing on an equal footing with the United States and Russia. That might have been the case. That was the case when the fighting stopped in 1945. But this Canadian government has been primarily responsible for preventing the commonwealth from being in that position today because, right from 1944, when the late Mr. Mackenzie King said that there would be no commonwealth bloc if he could prevent it, this government has been playing down the British commonwealth. By the actions of the ministry, one would think that they are trying to ease Canada out of the British commonwealth by the back door.

speechtext:
Then there is another 'thing. Let the Canadian government stop harrying- and I repeat the word "harrying"- the United States about Formosa. The action of the Americans with regard to Formosa is necessary for the maintenance of the defence line of the democracies in the Pacific. I have here a report of this speech by General MacArthur which the President would not allow to be delivered. What do we find? That great leader -and after all, he is the great leader in the Pacific area-described the chain of defence. The report states:
Through the Pacific victory of world war II, MacArthur said, the strategic frontier of the United States was extended from the coastal waters of the Americas "to embrace the entire Pacific ocean which has become a vast moat to protect us as long as we hold it ... We control it to the shores of Asia by a chain of islands extending in an arc from the Aleutians to the Marianas held by us and our free allies".
This natural chain is an easy defence line to maintain, MacArthur said, because it gives air domination of "every Asiatic port from Vladivostok to Singapore".
"If we hold this line we may have peace", MacArthur said, "... lose it and war is inevitable."
If that line goes, then the next line of defence on the Pacific will be not western Alaska but eastern Alaska, the Yukon, the Northwest Territories and Canada's west coast.
This question will be up for consideration in the United Nations within the next few days. I hope that the Canadian representatives will at least have the common sense and the decency to refrain from joining in the chorus attacking the United States about Formosa.
Another thought is this. Canada must help to bring about stability in the Pacific area. There is no collective security in the Pacific. Legally, the communists are able to run wild there without breaking any pact which can, in actual practice, get them into trouble. Suppose there is aggression in Indo-China, in the Malay peninsula or in Indonesia. The United Nations will not be able to act because the Russians have learned their lesson and are now back in the security council in a position to veto such action. The democracies were lucky to be able to get action in Korea but they cannot do that again through the security council. The North Atlantic treaty does not apply because it is restricted to stopping aggression in Europe or in North America.

Although I know that the Secretary of State for External Affairs continues to ridicule the idea, I suggest once more that Canada should take the lead in urging the setting up of a Pacific defence pact. Or if he is unwilling to do that, let him take the lead in advocating a broadening of the terms of the North Atlantic treaty so that they will cover aggression against a party to that treaty, no matter where in the world such aggression may take place. Furthermore, let him advocate that Australia and New Zealand be allowed to become parties to the North Atlantic treaty as well as any other democratic nation which cares to join.
Here is another thought. Canada must have larger forces in being, trained, and on a fire-brigade basis. Let us think of this as we would think of having a fire brigade in our own cities, quite apart from forces which are going overseas. It is so vital because Canada herself may be attacked. We are now facing that direct threat, and if we are attacked it will probably be without warning. That situation will continue, Mr. Speaker, just as long as this state of armed peace exists in the world. The crux of the problem is how long will it take to mobilize Canada's fighting divisions, and such units as her anti-aircraft regiments? At present that time can definitely be said to be a matter of months or perhaps of over a year.
We must have plans not only for the use of our fighting forces but also for our civil defence. The Minister of National Defence has not said one word about civil defence plans for Canada. We must have plans for industrial mobilization, for increasing our agricultural production, for the mobilization of our financial resources. Steps must be taken to root out profiteering. The government may not know it, but across this country today there is a wave of irresponsible price raising, which must be dealt with by parliament at this session. All these plans should be announced to us before the session is prorogued.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, all the war activities will bring about an increase in our national income. That is one good feature of this grim situation. The days ahead will be days of high employment. Now is the time to institute a system of contributory pensions and to abolish the means test. I realize that it could not be done at this session, but it certainly could be done at the next. Remember that in the second world war we were able to build up an unemployment insurance fund and put unemployment insurance on a solid basis in this country. I hope there will be no delay
The Address-Mr. Pearson in this move I am now recommending because nothing will do more to keep the morale of the Canadian people high in this time of crisis.
In conclusion, all of these steps Canada must now take will be difficult. They call for effort and sacrifices by our people. Above all they call for leadership by our government. The people of British Columbia are disturbed, as I have never seen them disturbed before, over the way in which this government has been floundering around since Canada went into the Korean era in the last week of June. People are disturbed at the way in which the government has been sitting back waiting to see which way public opinion would go.
In this new era, if Canada is to survive, her government must be courageous and must have clear-cut policies. There must be no more of this wobbling; the Canadian government must be ready at all times to give the Canadian people leadership.

If not, what states would he exclude and what states . would he include?
I do not think it is- desirable at this time to proceed along those lines in regard to security in the Pacific. In that position we have the approval and support of the government of the United States, of the government of the United Kingdom, of the government of India, and I have no reason to believe that the position of the government of Australia or that of the government of New Zealand is different.
We have of course obligations in regard to the Pacific. The operations in which we are engaged in Korea as a member of the United Nations show what these obligations are and that we accept them. But to add to the general obligations under the United Nations charter specific obligations of mutual defence in respect to other Pacific states at this time would, I suggest, Mr. Speaker, be a very rash course of policy for Canada.
The government has been strongly criticized in this debate by members of the official opposition because, in their words, we have not effectively carried out our obligations under the United Nations charter in respect of collective security. No member of the government and no member of this party will accept that charge for one moment. We reject the suggestion, and reject it with emphasis, that we have not done our duty in respect of Korea, and in respect of every other matter concerning collective security as a member of the United Nations.
We are criticized by members of the official opposition because we have not gone far enough in the discharge of our obligations in this particular matter. We have also been criticized by certain Independent members of


the house because we have gone too far. As usual, the position of the government, despite what members of the opposition may say, seems to represent a position of sanity and efficiency in the discharge of its obligations.
What we are doing in regard to Korea we are doing as a member of the United Nations, as I tried to say the other day, and in no other capacity. And in regard to certain criticism of the government that we have done too much-and I regret that the members who made that criticism are not present at this time-I would merely say that we had no choice in this matter, if we were to discharge our obligations to the United Nations and our obligations to our own national security, no choice but to join other states of the United Nations in the action which was decreed by the security council.
It has been suggested that we could have made further efforts in regard to mediation and the employment of pacific measures in this Korean dispute. That, of course, as I see it, is not a realistic suggestion. Because, even when it was tried-and it was tried in the early days of this dispute-the aggressor treated that suggestion with contempt. What we are doing on this occasion is to try to make it clear-and by "we" I mean the members who have accepted the security council resolution-that this time the aggressor will not be able to destroy his victims one by one, as he was able to do in 1938 and 1939. And in taking that action we hope that this lesson will be effectively learned where it needs to be learned, and that therefore we may not be asked later on to take more drastic action against those who are behind the aggression in Korea.
In that connection we feel that in the action we are taking in regard to Korea we are taking action not only for the defence of Canada but for the preservation of peace. And that brings me to a speech made in the house the other night by the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Pearkes).

speechtext: May I ask a question, for my own clarification? The minister states that this government is doing what he believes to be the correct thing according to our obligations under the United Nations. speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I shall try to answer the hon. member as I go along, because he has asked

a very important question. I do not know that I shall be able to satisfy him, but I shall do my best.
The hon. member for Nanaimo asked the other night, in a speech which I found very interesting-in fact, in a speech which, if it did not equal mine in the quantity of its adjectives, did include one or two nouns that we shall remember I think in this house long after my adjectives have been forgotten-he asked why did I skate around and not deal with the pathetic appeal from General MacArthur. And that point was made again this afternoon by other hon. members. Well, I did not do any skating around on this occasion at all because it was not necessary, and because no such appeal had been made.
The appeal to which the hon. member may have been referring, and which has been mentioned by other hon. members, was the appeal made by the Secretary General of the United Nations on July 14, which, as it has been stated, was made some weeks before this government made available, or put into operation, a set of circumstances which would make available land forces for Korea.
Now, that request of the secretary general was made on July 14. This government has been accused of delaying, and of lack of leadership, and of a lot of other things because we did not deal with it speedily and effectively enough. What was our obligation in regard to our position in the United Nations? What did we do to carry out that obligation?
Our obligation under the United Nations charter, as I understand it, is to accept the decision of the security council for the use of forces which have been made available to the United Nations by military agreements concluded between the countries concerned in the United Nations under article 43 of the charter. If this agreement had been concluded, then we would have been obliged, on account of the decision of the security council and after that decision had been discussed with us, to make any forces available to the security council which were covered by that agreement.
As it happened, for reasons which have been explained in this house, no such agreements have been made by any member of the United Nations. The Canadian government, as has been pointed out, took steps as far back as 1946 to urge upon the United Nations the desirability of making such an agreement, but no progress could be made because any discussion leading up to this had been vetoed, by the U.S.S.R., and all proposals were vetoed in the military staff committee by the representatives of the U.S.S.R. So we have no obligation on that score specifically
The Address-Mr. Pearson to send to the help of the United Nations armed forces which were covered by any agreement.
But that did not exempt us from the general obligation under the security council resolution to do what we could to restore peace and defeat aggression. We must accept that obligation. It is not a specific obligation to make any kind of forces available, but it is an obligation to do what we can to see that any aggression is defeated, once a security council resolution has been passed which we ourselves accept-as we did the security council resolution of June 29.
When this resolution was passed we did make help available to the United Nations and at once. As I said the other day, we made the three destroyers available. Shortly after that, on July 14, the secretary general made the appeal to which reference has been made, for further effective assistance, as he said- and I admit it-with ground forces.
Immediately after that the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) announced that we would make a transport squadron available. There was no intention on the part of the Canadian government at that time to make the first-line elements of the Canadian army available. That decision has been criticized by hon. members opposite. They have every right to criticize, if they wish; but we do not admit, having taken that position, that we were not discharging our obligations, in the light of subsequent developments.
What did we do then? Well, after announcing the dispatch of the R.C.A.F. transport squadron we entered into discussion at once with representatives of the unified command, and also with the secretary general, to find out not only what the situation in Korea was, but what it was likely to be, and what would be the use made of Canadian forces, and what would be the relationship of any contribution of ours on land to the possible extension of the conflict in Asia-to Formosa, for instance -and, particularly, what was the policy of the United States government in regard to such expansion. Was there any likelihood of a general expansion of this conflict in Korea in such a way that Canadian troops earmarked for Korea might be involved? To get some clarification of that point we discussed matters in London, Washington and at Lake Success. As I mentioned the other day, I made a trip to Washington where I had some very interesting and useful discussions with the secretary of state. I also made a trip to Lake Success. It was as a result of those explorations and of information which we were able to obtain that we made our further decision to send land forces on August 7 last,

The Address-Mr. Pearson less than a month after the secretary general had made his appeal to members of the United Nations.
It has been said that that was a dilatory and ineffective action on our part. As the hon. member for Nanaimo put it the other night, we should have given world leadership in this matter. Let us see what else we could have done and how we might have done it. Incidentally I should say that it was not until a week or ten days after that appeal of the secretary general that other countries began to make land forces available, countries such as Australia, New Zealand, the United Kingdom and some others. Among the countries that have responded effectively to the United Nations appeal Canada takes a proud place and does not need to apologize to anybody for her action.
When we are criticized for not doing enough and for not doing it quickly enough, then I think it is incumbent upon those who criticize us to tell us what might have been done, what alternative course might have been followed. This has been suggested on, the other side of the house. It has been suggested by the hon. member for Nanaimo, as I understood his speech, and this suggestion has been repeated by other hon. members opposite, that we should have sent the members of our permanent force to Korea at once to take part in the war going on there.
That was, not the course followed by our sister dominions of Australia and New Zealand. Indeed, it is not the course that was followed by other members of the United Nations who were in the circumstances in which we were placed. Of course it may be suggested that the United Kingdom has taken that course, having sent two battalions of its regular army to Korea. That is quite true. The United Kingdom made that decision some time after it had made an earlier decision to send a brigade. That decision may have been influenced by the fact that the United Kingdom had troops at Hong Kong, had a base of supplies at Hong Kong which would be able to supply troops sent from Hong Kong to Korea.
What could we have done if we had sent part or all of our permanent force to Korea when this request was made by the Secretary General of the United Nations? Is it suggested by any member opposite that our permanent mixed and trained brigade should have been sent at once to Korea as part of the United Nations forces there? If so, then I should think the worries of the hon. member for Nanaimo about the defence of the Pacific coast would have been much greater than they are now. That furthermore would


have been a course that was not followed by any other member of the United Nations. To the suggestion that we should give leadership, that would be getting far out in front of the parade. In a matter of this kind I do not think we want to be in that exposed position.
An alternative course was mentioned this afternoon by the hon,. member for Vancou-ver-Quadra (Mr. Green). The hon. member suggested that we should have sent part of our permanent force, I think he suggested one battalion, no doubt as a token contribution to the United Nations effort in Korea- one battalion to take part in operations seven or eight thousand miles away from its base of supply. I am certainly not a military expert, but I do not think that any military expert on this or on the other side of the house would seriously consider that possibility and would recommend that we should send a battalion at once to Korea and keep it supplied from a base seven or eight thousand miles away.

I think the best answer to that suggestion was given by the hon. member for Calgary East (Mr. Harkness) in his interesting speech the other night. I think I am quoting him correctly from Hansard when I say that he suggested that the western world cannot afford to commit its strength piecemeal in various parts of the world. I think that indicates a useful principle which should be applied, not only to Korea but to other areas where trouble may break out. Then the hon. member for Calgary East went on to ask the government whether they had any idea how they would meet further aggression like that we are facing today in Korea. I do not think we would be in a better position to meet such further aggression, aggression by proxy as it has been, called, if we had at the beginning of this aggression committed our active land forces at once to Korea. However, the question is a reasonable one and I think we should attempt to answer it.
I think it was the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. Higgins) who suggested when speaking the other night that we should have had a special force in readiness to carry out our United Nations obligations and have been able to send troops to Korea at once without danger of denuding our defences on this continent. Other hon. members opposite have asked why we had not made plans of that kind. As I tried to say the other night, no member of the

United Nations, including the United States of America and Great Britain, had plans of that kind in readiness to meet aggression.
For reasons which to me seem pretty clear, we did not contemplate this kind of aggression. I admitted that the other day and a good deal has been made of that admission. Why did we not expect it? In the first place, we did not expect it because there were no military agreements under article 43 by which we were bound. In the second place, we did not expect it because it was difficult to visualize a resolution of the security council to use force against a communist state which would not be vetoed by the U.S.S.R. as a member of the security council. Therefore, realizing the weaknesses of the security council in this matter, realizing the unlikelihood of the United Nations being able to live up to its joint obligations in respect to this kind of aggression, certainly from communist countries, we had along with other countries worked out the North Atlantic pact under which our obligations in respect of that group of states would be specific and would not be vetoed by anybody.
It has been asked this afternoon whether any plans have been made to meet aggression under the North Atlantic pact. It was suggested in one statement that if we were not ready for Korea we might not foe ready for Norway. I submit that the situation is different indeed. For the last year under the North Atlantic pact we have been working out plans to meet aggression against any member of the north Atlantic community. Canada's contribution to those plans is being worked out. It is being discussed, and when the discussions are completed the result will foe announced to this house.
But I am sure hon. members will appreciate that it is very difficult indeed at this time, in the midst of these discussions, to explain in detail what part we may have to play in regard to the carrying out of our obligations under the North Atlantic pact. It is possible, however-and I am sure the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) will not mind if I say this-to say at this time, pending revision of those plans which is now under way in the light of developments since June, that it is understood by our friends of the North Atlantic pact that our position in regard to collective defence in an attack on western Europe would be, on land, to use our permanent force to assist United States forces, or to foe assisted by United States forces, in repelling a direct attack from the north, and using it as a basis for the expansion of our army for a later expeditionary force to defend Canada outside Canada.
That was stated the other day. That has been stated by the Minister of National
The Address-Mr. Pearson Defence. That is our general position inside the North Atlantic plan. If and when that position may be altered-and it may be altered in the light of developments and we may have to do other things-that change will be announced.

Mr. Speaker, I tried to deal with that, but no doubt not to the satisfaction of the hon. member. I said that during the intervening period we had been making investigations in Washington, London, at Lake Success, and indeed elsewhere, as to what would be the likelihood of the conflict in Korea extending to other countries in the Far East, what particularly was going to be the policy of the United States with respect to communist China and Formosa, and things of that kind. During that time these investigations were made, and after they were completed the government took the decision announced on August 7.
I should say in regard to north Atlantic developments that, as I mentioned the other night, the north Atlantic council is to meet in New York a week from this coming Saturday, and it may well be that important decisions will be taken at that meeting. During the last four or five weeks, the deputies of the north Atlantic council members have been meeting almost continuously in London to revise plans for supply, plans for strengthening forces in being, and to revise plans for mutual aid in the light of the situation which has developed since June. There has been an urgency attached to these meetings which possibly did not exist before June. If that is true, all members of the north Atlantic council must take their fair share of responsibility, but there is no doubt that what we had been planning to do before June, to be brought to completion say in a year, a year and a half or two years, is now being planned for completion at an earlier date. Behind all this planning is the desire, and indeed the determination, of the north Atlantic countries to get forces in being in western Europe at the earliest possible date.

The Address-Mr. Pearson
In that connection I was a little worried by the suggestion made by the hon. member for Calgary East (Mr. Harkness) the other night. I do not want to misrepresent what he said, but as I understood him it was almost a gospel of despair in regard to the defence of the outlying members of the western European community, and that we should fall back on the Pyrenees. We shall never be able to build up a north Atlantic system on that basis. If we cannot give the members of the north Atlantic community and western Europe the hope that this time they will not have to be liberated but that the enemy can be defeated before their countries are occupied, we shall not be in as strong a position as we should be to meet any attack with our allies.

and we cannot defend ourselves without their help-we have to give them the conviction that this time they are not going to be subjected to liberation.
Reference was made this afternoon by the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green) to the formation of a British commonwealth division, as he called it, and the use of the Canadian special brigade in that division. I thought the Minister of National Defence made our position pretty clear on that matter the other afternoon. This brigade from Canada is to be a part of the United Nations forces in Korea if at the time when its training is completed that is the place where it should go. In that connection maybe I should say once again that the brigade is being earmarked not merely for Korea but to carry out our United Nations obligations, where-ever those obligations may arise. If at the time their training is completed Korea is the place, that is the place to which they will go. If it is not Korea, then they will go somewhere else. In that respect we have undertaken to carry out our United Nations commitments, in a way, as I understand it, that no other member of the United Nations has yet done. '
This is a question which I think will be discussed at the forthcoming United Nations assembly. We think that in acting as we have done in respect to the formation of a special brigade, we have started something very important, the importance of which is much


broader than Korea. We think that by this precedent we have begun the establishment of United Nations forces for use not only in Korea but elsewhere. In making their contributions to Korea, we hope that other countries will make them in that form so that the next time this kind of aggression by proxy takes place there will be forces in being not only in Canada but in other countries to deal with such aggression. Of course making our special brigade available to the United Nations in that way does not remove the problem of how it is to be used in Korea if it goes there.
It has been suggested by hon. members opposite that it should become a part of a British commonwealth division. So far as I am concerned, 1 feel that the operation in Korea is not a United States operation. It is not a British commonwealth operation. It is not an operation of members of the British commonwealth. It is a United Nations operation. We have made this brigade available to the United Nations. We have already been discussing with the unified command in Korea-which is in fact in Washington- how the brigade may best be used to accomplish the purpose which we all have in mind. If the parliament of Canada gives consent to our proposal that it should be used for carrying out a United Nations Obligation, the unified command will decide how this brigade is to be used. If the unified command says our Canadian brigade, armed with British-type equipment and accustomed to serving with troops in the commonwealth- as the hon. gentleman has said, one could not serve with better troops-should serve with troops from the commonwealth, that is where that brigade will go. They will be very proud indeed to go there, along with their comrades from Australia, New Zealand, and the United Kingdom.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. gentleman has raised an important and difficult question indeed. The hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra paid General MacArthur an eloquent tribute this afternoon, and .1 should like to associate myself with it. General MacArthur is now serving in somewhat of a dual capacity. He is the commander of the United States occupation forces in Japan, and in that capacity he receives his orders from the commander in chief of the United States, who is the president. He has also received authority from the security council to exercise command over United Nations forces available for operations in Korea. In that capacity he receives instructions and advice from the security council of the United Nations. The largest portion of the United Nations forces in Korea at the present time are United States forces, and General MacArthur is also commander of those United States forces. In that capacity he gets his instructions from the President of the United States. I do not know whether or not that clarifies the issue. I am inclined to * doubt whether the position can be clarified.
Other points have arisen in the debate on this subject with which I should deal. I hope to do so rather briefly. The hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) made two very useful comments this morning during the course of his eloquent speech. Those comments concerned improving the procedure in the United Nations assembly so that, if at any time in the future there should be a representative of the U.S.S.R. on the security council when a resolution such as the Korean matter came before the council, and it were 69262-15
The Address-Mr. Pearson vetoed, the United Nations would still be able to act to preserve peace. He has suggested that we should improve our procedure with regard to an emergency session of the general assembly, and also that there might well be a commission of that assembly as a permanent agency charged with supervising questions of peace and security. Those are two useful ideas. They have already been advanced by other members of the United Nations within the last few weeks, looking forward to the forthcoming meeting of the assembly. We are discussing them with friendly governments and it may well foe that, as a result of the forthcoming meeting of the assembly, some progress along that line can be made.
The hon. member for Lake Centre also asked me straightforwardly this morning what attitude the government of Canada had taken when the Schuman plan was announced in London last May. The Schuman plan, that wise and imaginative act of French statesmanship, was not one which concerned this government directly. I believe that though we should naturally give leadership wherever it is desirable to give leadership, we should not always be handing out gratuitous advice in matters of this kind to countries whose responsibility in respect of these matters is greater than ours. So we would have to be rather careful of any comments we might make to the United Kingdom government. As it happens, we did informally tell them we thought this was an important and far-reaching plan, the importance of which was possibly greater politically than economically, and that whatever the economic difficulties may be in carrying it out-further consideration of that plan has shown that there will be great difficulty in carrying it out-it would be unwise for any government not to fall in at once with the principle behind this plan to further the integration, politically and economically, of the western European countries. It would be unwise especially not to do everything to encourage the French in any proposal which may heal the age-long conflict between the French and the Teutons. In that sense possibly we did interfere, but it was merely giving the United Kingdom government, if they considered it to be of benefit, the benefit of our general views in respect to this matter. I believe the attitude which western European governments have adopted subsequently to this proposal shows that is the line being taken by them all.
In this debate a great deal has been said about the fact that, while the government makes fine statements, it does not do very much to carry them out. In so far as defence is concerned, I leave the answer to that charge

The Address-Mr. Pearson to my friend the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton). In so far as information is concerned, I do not admit-I know he will not admit-that we are open to the accusation of not giving the house all the information that is proper with regard to the matters with which we are charged. So far as external affairs are concerned I have nothing to apologize for in that respect. As the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra said this afternoon, picking up a white paper from the Department of External Affairs which he found useful in developing his argument, "This tells the whole story". I am glad he found it helpful. In the future it will continue to be our policy, as it has been in the past, to give him all the information we can so that he may be in a position to develop his argument in the light of the whole story. One of these days we may produce a white paper on the Pacific pact, to which we shall ask him to write an appendix.

speechtext:
It has been stated in regard to the economic and social aspects of this question that we talk well but do little. In fact I have been in the happy if at times embarrassing position of listening to my speeches being quoted back at me with every manifestation of approval by certain members of the C.C.F. group. I am not inclined, of course, to take back one word I have said in those speeches, and as other members of the government have said, as to the importance of parallel economic and social action with defence action. The two must go together. I said the other day, and I repeat now, that I hope that we shall never be in a position in this country where defence action is of such a character and of such an extent that we shall not be able to make progress in the direction of social and economic improvement.
But then it has been stated, and the criticism was fairly direct, that while I gave lip service to the necessity of extending this principle in our relations wth other countries, we had done little in the United Nations in that regard. I would ask hon. members to look up the record of Canada in the United Nations. If they do so, I think they will be agreed that our record has not been a bad one; nor have we defaulted on our social and economic obligations in the world assembly.
Our record with regard to post-war relief and rehabilitation is well known. Our record in humanitarian causes there is well known. We were the third largest subscriber to the United Nations children's emergency fund.

We have actively participated in the development of the four point program. In our appropriation last year we also made an interim contribution to that program.
We admit that it will be of no great and permanent value if we defeat the communist armies in the field and do not help to remove in those countries the causes which have made easy communist aggression against them. We shall have to do something in this field, and we shall no doubt be considering that matter at the next United Nations assembly. I do not think that Canada will be behind others in the part that she plays in that field. But there is something I would point out to some of the hon. members who have been most critical in that regard, especially in regard to aid to southeast Asia which we are actively pursuing at the moment and concerning which is meeting in London in a couple of weeks a conference which will be attended by a member of the Canadian government.
I would point out that while we should, and no doubt will, play our proper part in aid to southeast Asia and to other materially underdeveloped countries, those countries themselves should do everything in their power to raise the standards of living of their own people. That means strong and stable government, government as strong and stable as they can find in the present circumstances. It also means that they should devote some of their resources to economic and social development.
For western countries which are bearing quite a heavy burden in the defence against communism, which is a defence not only against communism in our own countries but against communism in their countries, it is a little bit discouraging at times to look around and see in some of these Asian countries what a high proportion of their budget is devoted, not to social and economic progress but to defence itself. In some of the countries that we should like most to help, more than half their present budget is devoted to national defence. If that budget of theirs could be reduced from 50 per cent for national defence to 25 per cent, the need for help from us would not be nearly so great. We are obliged to take that fact into consideration, of course, in trying to assist them.
I have only one further observation to make, Mr. Speaker. More than one speaker opposite has accused this government of complacency and of ministering to that feeling by its statements to parliament and to the country. I do not know of any statements of the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent), of the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) or of myself which could be

charged as being responsible for encouraging any feeling of complacency in this country in the face of what we are up against. We know what we are up against. I could quote statement after statement of the Prime Minister and of other members of the government designed to bring home to the people of this country a realization of what we are up against; andi similar statements have been, made by hon. gentlemen opposite.
This afternoon the hon. member for Van-couver-Quadra criticized strongly indeed the Prime Minister's statement last Friday as being too complacent because he said that the next ten months will be the critical period, that if we can get through those ten months it might be easier in the future and we might look forward to a long period of at least a twilight zone between peace and war. If I may say so, with all respect, Mr. Speaker, I think the Prime Minister is absolutely right. It may not be ten months. It may be eight months. It may be eighteen months. But the year or year and a half ahead is the dangerous period; and if we can get through that period, we may then have time to settle our problems even with those people behind the iron curtain.
If the Prime Minister's statement ministered to complacency and is designed to throw dust in the eyes of our people, what about the statement made at the same time by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew)? I quote from that statement, and I do not object to these words at all, but no doubt the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra may object to them. The leader of the official opposition said this, and I am quoting from his statement as reported at page 115 of Hansard:
I have said that I have great hope.
We all say "Amen" to that.
I believe that hope on my part was increased through some of the contacts I had within the past few weeks.
Then in the concluding paragraph he said, and I again quote from Hansard, at page 116:
I believe, Mr. Speaker, that we may well be coming to freedom's crowning hour.
I think those were fine and inspiring words on the part of the leader of the opposition, but they were no finer and no more inspiring than the words of our Prime Minister.

Yes, Mr. Speaker, I quite agree that the hon. member did say that. But I think that if he reads the Prime Minister's statement and if the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra reads it, they will realize that anything that the Prime Minister said in that respect was also conditional on doing all that we can and should do.
We may have differences in this house, Mr. Speaker, as to how we should do these things, but we have no differences in any part of the house about the fact that they should be done. Our best chance for peace now-and we have all said this so often that it is becoming platitudinous, but it is like so many other platitudes, which become platitudes because they are so true-is in preparation. If we can arm, militarily, economically and socially, to a point where we can convince an aggressor that he has nothing to gain but everything to lose by aggression, then we may get time, and during that time we may be able to take steps which may lead to more permanent peace; because the whole history of humanity shows, if it shows nothing else, that there can be no permanent peace on the basis of armed strength alone. All we can hope for now is a breathing space; and we shall never get a breathing space unless we can convince an aggressor-that is, all of us in this country and other countries-that we are strong enough to defeat aggression.
Maybe we are not strong enough to do that now. But I would remind hon. members that we have strength in the western community, apart from the strength on the land, on the water and in the air. We have strength in regard to our scientific developments; and that strength is standing between us now, possibly, and aggression. While that situation lasts we may be safe. But it will not last for ever. During that time we must build up other forms of strength. If we can do that, we may be safe. If we cannot do that, none of us is complacent about the future. A great scientist-a very great scientist indeed, Mr. Speaker-and a man who knew something not only about science but about war, was asked the other day as to how he thought the next war would be fought. Would it be a pushbutton war? Would it be a purely scientific war? Or would it be a war of the traditional kind? And his answer was: "I do not know what weapons we shall use in the next war, but I know what weapons we shall use in the war after that-rocks".

speechtext:
I never misinterpret anybody. The hon. member, I think, left himself open on certain points in his speech. However, I am only going to refer to one or two things which, perhaps, are of minor importance.
Criticism has been made of Canada's unreadiness at this time of need. I would say that that is unfortunate, but I do not believe it is to our discredit. We are in the position of all the western nations, in that after the war we thought we could demobilize our armies and give our attention and our resources to building up the economic and social needs of our people and, as far as we could, of other people as well. If we haven't done all that we should, I believe we haven't done too badly. Now, because we have done that we are meeting this difficult situation without the arms and the men that we might have had if we had applied ourselves, as the Soviet union has done, to arming ourselves first and looking after the economic needs of our people afterwards. I believe if we keep that in mind it will obviate at least a part of our criticism; and that is desirable, because, as the Secretary of State for External Affairs said just before he took his seat, we are all in general agreement in this house on the main purpose for which we have come here, namely, to stop aggression in Korea. Any differences we may have on details- though they may be substantial-are small in comparison with that agreement.
I mentioned our unpreparedness. I want to say that it frightens me to hear people in this country and in other countries continually harping on our unpreparedness. If the Soviet union pays any attention to what we say-and I would hope that she does-then she must be convinced by now that there is no possible chance of our being able to defend ourselves. Consequently, broadcasting our weakness is an invitation to her to attack. I would suggest that we stop blazoning to the world our unpreparedness to defend ourselves and get busy with building our defences both military and economic.

May I say just one word about another matter mentioned by the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra, and in reply to him, by the Secretary of State for External Affairs, namely, General MacArthur? After listening to the explanation of his position by the Secretary of State for External Affairs I am quite satisfied that General MacArthur is a very important man in a very important position. But I have been watching him for many years. As a matter of fact, I had the honour of sitting in at a conference at one time in which he was the leading figure, and I am satisfied that General MacArthur is convinced that he receives instructions from a higher authority than the President of the United States, and because he believes that he often acts on it.
I should like to comment on the reference made by the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra to the Highland regiments and their place in the force that we would send to Korea, and his proposal that there should be a commonwealth force. I am sorry that those points should be raised at this time, because if there is anything that is required today it is that the armies fighting in Korea should be more a United Nations force and not less. The criticism one hears on every hand is that this is a United States war. If we are to obviate that criticism the force fighting in Korea will have to be not a United States army or a commonwealth army, but a United Nations army in every respect.
As to the place of Highland regiments, no one is more proud of the Highlanders as fighting men than I am. Whether they will be in a separate regiment limited to themselves and the bagpipes, or whether they are fighting with other soldiers in the United Nations army, I am sure they will give a good account of themselves, and that is the important thing in any war.
I mentioned that in this house we are all agreed on the main purpose that brought us here. I am not going to engage in any criticism that would indicate that I have any difference of opinion on that point, because I have not. I should like to emphasize the point made by the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) when he spoke in the debate the other evening and told us that we should make it more clear to the people of Canada than we have done so far as to why we are in Korea, and why we must be there until the aggressors are defeated. I am sure they are not clear on the issue, and there is a great deal of propaganda circulated to confuse them.
The evening before I left home to come here I received a telephone call from a young

man who said he wanted to make an appointment to see me. He did not state the purpose of his visit. I set an appointed hour, and he came in company with five or six other young people between the ages of about twenty and twenty-seven or twenty-eight. He stated as the purpose of his visit that he wanted to [DOT] know what my views were on the Korean war. I found out soon that they belonged to a communist youth organization. What would amaze anyone with whom these young people talked is how well they were briefed on what to say-plausible arguments as to why we should not be helping the United States in a civil war in Korea.
Before their arrival another man left a leaflet almost the size of half a page of a newspaper at my door. The purposes of the leaflet was to convince people why they should sign the so-called Stockholm peace petition. Those leaflets would be left at the door of every house not only in Vancouver, but in every city in Canada.
In my opinion the government and those who agree with the government's policy have not taken as much time to make the position of Canada clear as these people are taking to confuse it by the use of lies, half-lies, and scarcely any truth at all. I suggest to the government that that must be done, because in a democratic country more than military equipment and a fighting force is required. We will have to have the understanding and support of the people in every community in Canada, because if we do not have that there will be confusion of thought of which our opponents will take advantage on every possible occasion.
I decided to speak along this line because my attention has been focused in that direction by reading the reports of war correspondents in the field and other correspondents who are watching this situation. In my opinion we should without delay answer some of the questions people are asking. What are our intentions in Korea? If we succeed in driving the North Koreans back to the 38th parallel, are we going to stop there or are we going to go on beyond that? As this is a United Nations force, I agree that it is not altogether within our right to say what a United Nations army is going to do when it reaches that point; but our government certainly should make it clear what is their opinion on the issue.
Thomas J. Hamilton, New York Times staff correspondent at Lake Success, raises the question in an article which appears in the
The Address-Mr. Maclnnis News-Herald of Vancouver on August 25. Writing on this subject he says:
It has been assumed that once the entire peninsula is under United Nations control, the next thing would be to hold elections to decide the further government, and Austin's speech revealed that the United States wants them to be held on the basis that the Republic of Korea's jurisdiction would be extended over North Korea automatically.
I suggest to those who feel that the United Nations forces should go beyond the 38th parallel that if we want to start a third world war that would be the best way to start it. The Soviet union may not move into this fight until an attempt is made-if it is made-to cross that boundary. But surely no one can be so naive as to expect that the Soviet union would give up any jurisdiction or any influence it considers it has by arrangement or by treaty, and allow the forces of the United Nations to go beyond the 38th parallel.
I suggest that point should be made clear, and that the government should state where it stands in the matter. It should be made *clear before we ask our soldiers to enlist.
In regard to holding an election in the whole of Korea this correspondent states, in the same article:
The difficulty is that there is a strong probability that this would result in an over-all communist majority if the elections were held before the communization of North Korea had been undone, and before a United Nations reconstruction program had assuaged the bitterness of North and South Korea against the destruction of their homes during their liberation by United Nations forces. In that case communism would win by an election what it failed to obtain by an invasion.
That is important, too, because it puts before us the point emphasized by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) on Thursday and again today, and which has been emphasized repeatedly in the house by various speakers, that if we win a victory by arms and do nothing else to build the economy of that country, to set the people free from their exploiters, we have lost the war, no matter what military victories we may have achieved. I suggest to the government that those are important points.
I should like to refer to another matter which has been mentioned in this debate by a number of speakers and which wa^ referred to particularly by the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green). I refer to Formosa. I listened with interest to the statement of the Secretary of State for External Affairs in that regard and I agree completely with it, as do all the members of the group with which I am associated. It has been suggested that Chiang Kai-shek should be told to get out of Formosa and the people permitted to freely elect their own government. That is a fine sentiment, and no one

The Address-Mr. Maclnnis would be more pleased to see it carried out than I, but there is no possibility of its happening. No sooner would Chiang get out than the communists would come in.

Would it not be wisdom for this country now, before our backs are to the wall, to forget about shorter hours, and to go to a forty-four or forty-eight hour week? The price of freedom is, in my opinion, not money, but production.
May I go this far with my hon. friend and say that I am convinced, not just because a war is being waged, that the greatest need not only of Canada but of the world today is greater production. The next greatest need is better distribution of that production. Unless we have better distribution we shall not have more wealth to distribute. No trade union leader or anyone else can tell the workers today to produce more unless he can assure them that, not only in war but also in peace, the more they work the more they will have and the better off they will be. That has not been the experience of the workers. As far back as their memory goes, their experience has been that they are poor not when goods are scarce but when [DOT] goods are plentiful, because it is then they are unemployed. It is then that they have to sell their labour for what employers are willing to pay.
If you can assure the worker that the more he produces the better off he will be, the more he will have, the better the clothes his family will have, and the better he can educate his children, I am sure you will have no difficulty with the worker. I am also sure that there is no other way to make an attack on mass poverty, not of distant parts or undeveloped countries, but the mass poverty in Canada. There is no other way to make a mass attack except by increasing the production of those things that are useful to us, and then by more equitable distribution. I hope that before the session is over the people of Canada may have some assurance that their wages will buy as much next week as they bought this week, and that they will buy as much the week after, and the week after that. If we do not do so we are going to be faced with a lot of trouble. It will not do to say that there is a war on, and that we ought to be patriotic. There are sufficient resources, sufficient skill and sufficient labour in this country to keep up our standard of living, and to keep up our social services, even while we are preparing for a war and even while we are engaged in a war. I do not say that that could continue over a long period of time. As a matter of fact the world will soon be confronted with an inability to carry on a war because of a lack of resources due to the rate at which war consumes certain essential

The Address-Mr. Maclnnis
resources. But we have in Canada the resources to keep up our standard of living, and to improve the standard of living of the lower paid groups; to keep up our social services and still to provide for war. If we< organize our human and material resources properly, all that can be accomplished. If we do not do that, let me say again that we are in for trouble.
I should like to draw attention to a press release sent out by the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gregg) on August 29. This release refers to the improved employment picture for men. Then there is this paragraph:
The employment picture for women was not quite so favourable. At August 17, there were 56,000 applications for employment from women on hand with the national employment service. This amounted to 3.5 per cent of the women in the labour force and was 14,600 higher than a year ago. The increase in the number of women looking for work is explained in part by the decline in employment in the textiles and service industries from last year, and in part by the greater number of married women seeking work today.
Why do married women seek work? Essentially, married women seek work because the head of the family does not bring in sufficient income to feed and clothe the family. That may not always be the case. It may not be the case where there is no family. But where there is a family, I am satisfied that 999 mothers out of every 1,000 want to be with their families and not looking for work in a factory or anywhere else.
At the beginning of this session we had a matter before us concerning labour. I have been impressed, not just this session and not just this year, with all the legal processes that labour must go through before it can get an increase in the price of the commodity it has to sell. How easy it is for others to raise the price of their commodities. I noticed in the newspapers that the rubber companies increased the price of rubber twice within the last few weeks. There was an increase of seven per cent and then an increase of fifteen per cent in the price of passenger car tires and an increase of twenty per cent in the price of truck tires. I did not hear of any conciliation board or any arbitration board being set up to pass on these increases or to find out if they were necessary. The prices were raised, and the rest of us went on paying the increased prices. There was no question about how much this would increase the cost of living for others. But let the worker ask for four cents an hour and it takes him fourteen months of negotiations, conciliation boards, et cetera, if he lives that long, as well as other desperate actions before he can get it. Similar increases are taking place in the price of sugar, of meat, and other essential things we use. I ask this government what they are going to do to protect the people of Canada.

I am supporting them in everything they want to do in Korea to protect the world, but I do not believe we should forget our own people at home.
