speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the leader of this group spoke in this debate he stated that we would support the building up of a special force to be placed at the disposal of the security council in order to meet our general commitments to the United Nations Organization. It is largely on that matter that I wish to speak tonight.
First of all, I may state that we in this group have no intention of trying to make any political capital out of the present situation because we consider that the matter is altogether too serious for that kind of thing; and we feel that every member should do everything in his power at this time to help the government in a constructive way. As a matter of fact, what I have to say tonight will be largely what I have already stated in my constituency during a series of meetings that I held prior to this session.
When South Korea was attacked by the North Korean forces the Secretary General of the United Nations approached the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) for a ground force to be sent to Korea; and as we all know, the Prime Minister refused to send a ground force at that time. For that he was severely criticized by a portion of the press both in this country and in the United States. Nevertheless I feel that the Prime Minister was absolutely justified in the stand that he took, because we had only one brigade of trained troops. It is all very well to say that we should have had more, but we must face the situation as it is and not as it might have been. Had we sent that brigade to Korea, and had it become engaged in battle and suffered severe losses, we of course would not have had the necessary reinforcements to send to it. Then again, we have specific commitments under the North Atlantic treaty, and that brigade is needed in Canada to fulfil those commitments and also for the defence of Canada.
I do not want to see another Hong Kong where ill-trained and ill-equipped men were sent into battle. I think it is extremely important that any men who are sent out of this country shall be properly trained and properly equipped, and that no man should be sent from the country until he has reached that degree of perfection.

It will be recalled that, at the time the United Nations Organization was first set up, we in this group expressed lack of confidence in its ability to maintain peace; and at that time we gave a number of reasons why we felt that way. I am going to refer to only one or two of the reasons tonight, but they are reasons that I think are just as strong today as they were then.
First of all, we felt that some of the more powerful nations that were supporting the United Nations Organization lacked either the will or the desire to implement policies that were absolutely essential to the maintenance of peace. I listened with interest to the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) when he stated that you cannot hope to defeat communism by force of arms alone, that you must have economic and social reforms and that economic aid must be granted to the weaker nations. I agree with that statement wholeheartedly. But my mind goes back to the year 1944 when we were discussing proposals for international finance and trade policies to be instituted in the post-war world; we were discussing the matter in the reconstruction committee at the time, and the deputy minister of finance was one of the main witnesses.
We took the stand that lend-lease and mutual aid should be continued in the postwar world in order to help to bring about the rehabilitation of the devastated areas and that, when that task had been completed, there would then be an obligation on the part of the western world to accept freely from the European nations exports in exchange for her exports to them. I recall that at that time that suggestion was criticized by the deputy minister of finance as being idealistic. I wonder if any ministers of the government would still take that stand or support the deputy minister of finance by saying that that is an idealistic stand to take today? As a matter of fact, I think the government has moved quite a long way in that direction. Unfortunately, however, we are still falling far short of implementing policies that will make it possible to distribute surpluses to needy nations.
It will be recalled that the food and agriculture organization was set up under the United Nations Organization. Various members of that organization from time to time have stressed the fact that never again would nations tolerate a situation in which food was destroyed or in which the production of food was curtailed, so long as there were starving people in the world. The FAO, in order to deal with that very situation, brought down a proposal that would have made it possible
The Address-Mr. Quelch to distribute surplus foods to needy nations. It was termed the international commodity clearing house. Unfortunately, that proposal was turned down by the FAO conference. Unfortunately, also, Canada voted against that proposal.
Yet what is the situation? Even as late as last year, the United States had surplus foods to the amount of about $4 billion. A great deal of that food rotted or was destroyed. Even here in Canada the farmers of western Canada this spring were urged to reduce their acreage of wheat by three million acres because there might be a surplus of wheat. When the chairman of the wheat board was before the committee on agriculture, I askedi him whether or not, in his opinion, there was any danger of a surplus of wheat, having regard to the actual needs of the nations of the world. He said no. Then he went on to say that having regard to the ability of the nations to pay us in the type of exchange that we wanted for that wheat, there might be a surplus.
I just cite that example to show that we are still a long way from solving the problem of getting our surplus food to needy people. It is all very well to talk about the need for increasing production in the world today; but it is of little use to increase the production of food unless at the same time you take steps to ensure that that food can be distributed to the people who need it. Just imagine what the reaction of the people in Asia must be when they read of large surpluses of food accumulating in the western world and of that food being allowed to rot while at the same time there are millions of people starving in Asia. In that regard I say the government is long on words and short on actions, because when the proposal for an international commodity clearing house was put before them the representatives of this government turned it down without, mind you, having any alternative proposal whereby surplus food could be got to needy nations.
When the United Nations Organization was first set up we heard, and even today we hear, a lot of talk about the United Nations Organization providing for collective security. I would say that there is no security under the United Nations Organization. All it provides for is collective action, and collective action and collective security are two different things.
Even at the time we were discussing the setting up of the United Nations Organization it was becoming quite evident that the world was becoming divided into two separate
234	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Quelch camps, the communist camp and the anticommunist camp, or, shall we say, the democratic camp. And each of those camps was doing everything in its power to collect as many other nations to its support as possible. The U.S.S.R. were depending largely upon encouraging minority groups to overthrow governments, to get their help. We were depending largely, to put it crudely, upon a form of economic bribery. That is to say, we promised certain nations that if they signed certain agreements with us we would grant them economic aid. And therefore today we have a situation where instead of one world that we heard so much about at one time, we have two distinct worlds, two distinct camps, the communist camp and the anti-communist camp, and both of these camps today are doing everything in their power to build up their armed forces.
With a situation like that, how can anybody talk about collective security? We are back practically to the old idea of balance of power. Each of these camps is trying to build up a balance of power that would be greater than that of the other camp. If war does come, does anybody think that the preparation so made will possibly provide for security? Win or lose, it will mean the wholesale destruction of cities in both camps and the wholesale slaughter of thousands or millions of people. Therefore the word "security" is altogether the wrong type of word to use in regard to that matter.
The government has been charged with a lack of preparedness. But when that charge is made I always keep in mind the fact that the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) did everything in his power, when he was secretary of state for external affairs, to get the member nations of the United Nations Organization to agree definitely to commit themselves to provide armed forces toward an international force, and up to this year no nation, apparently, had been willing to commit itself. Therefore, largely as a result of the failure of the United Nations Organization to set up an international army which could be placed at the disposal of the security council, we had the Atlantic treaty signed, under which twelve nations agreed to come to each other's assistance in the event of aggression. And it is of course under that treaty that we have specific commitments. That is one reason, as I have already said, that I thought the Prime Minister was absolutely justified in refusing to send to Korea the one brigade we had.
We often hear, and we have heard during this session, the question asked, what are we fighting for in Korea? I must admit that I am not satisfied with most of the declarations 

that have been made. Some hon. members suggested that we are fighting to free Korea. I wonder whether that is the reason. I wonder, if a free expression of thought could have been taken from the Koreans as a whole as to whether or not they wanted us to intervene, whether they would have said yes, knowing full well that intervention by us must mean the wholesale destruction of their towns, their villages, their railways, their assets and the slaughter of thousands upon thousands of civilians. I think probably they . would have considered the cost too high, and said that they were not prepared to defend their so-called freedom at that price. Even if we win the war, have they any assurance that they will really have freedom? No, Mr. Speaker, I think the real thing that we are fighting for in this war is to try to create a prestige for the United Nations Organization that they have never had in the past. That is, that it was a warning to the communist nations that in future any acts of aggression by them against any one of the members of the United Nations Organization will be met by force. That in itself may help to prevent acts of aggression against other nations, but in the meantime I would say that Korea is having to be the goat in the case.
It is all very well for people to say it is better to fight in Korea than in Canada. From our point of view that is so, but from the point of view of the people of Korea I do not think they are anxious that the fight should take place in their country. They would just as soon have the fight carried on in another part of the world.
On the other hand, I think we have to avoid the danger of having our forces dissipated over too great an area. It seems to me that if we should spread our forces over too great an area of the world we shall be playing right into the hands of the U.S.S.R. It has been suggested that the communist forces never expected the United Nations Organization to intervene in Korea. The fact that they have such large forces there shows quite clearly,
I would say, that even if they did not expect it they were fully prepared for that eventuality. I feel that that is actually what they were hoping for. The war in Korea may be merely looked upon as a first move on the checkerboard, to be followed by subsequent moves. In dealing with that first move we must keep in mind that there will be other moves that we shall have to deal with in the future, and we must maintain our forces in such a way that we shall be ready to meet subsequent moves.
Apparently the Prime Minister looks upon the next ten months as the critical ones, and
23S

then expects a long period without war. The Secretary of State for External Affairs referred to that this afternoon and pointed out that in reality the Prime Minister was agreeing with what the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) had already said. I hope the Prime Minister is right when he says that after the war in Korea is brought to a successful conclusion we may look for a long period of peace. On the other hand, if the war in Korea is finished within ten months I would say it will only be because the U.S.S.R. and China have not participated.
If the U.S.S.R. and China come to the support of northern Korea, then I do not think that anyone would suggest for one minute that that war would be over in ten months. If the U.S.S.R. and China keep out of the Korean war it will mean that at the end of the Korean war the forces of the U.S.S.R. and China will be intact. Therefore one would be extremely optimistic to look for a long period of peace after Korea, whilst the tremendous forces of the U.S.S.R. and China are intact; unless in the meantime we are able to reach a better understanding with these countries.
I think an important step that must be taken is to establish economic and trade policies that will provide not only for the maximum production of food, but for its distribution to the needy peoples of the world. For so long as you have starvation in any part of the world you have a fertile breeding ground for communism. We have done a lot of talking about that question in the last five years, but have made very little progress toward its solution, and practically no progress so far as Asia is concerned.
In other words, we cannot hope to build a lasting peace upon a foundation of economic war, such as we have had even in the last five years, since the end of the second world war. Therefore I agree with the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) that we should demonstrate to the world what can be done by a democratic country blessed with great natural resources.
In order to bring about the maximum production that is so essential for our war effort and for the establishment of peace, I believe certain steps are absolutely essential at this time. First of all, in my view, price controls and subsidies should be established immediately in order to keep down the cost of living and to ensure fair prices to primary producers, as well as to prevent further labour disputes, because undoubtedly the high cost of living is one of the chief causes of labour unrest at the present time. Then I believe the government should go ahead with its irrigation program. I know it is 69262-16j
The Address-Mr. Quelch being said in many places that, now that war has come, we have to increase our defence expenditures, and that such things as irrigation will have to be held in abeyance. But if it is so important to maintain the maximum production of food, then irrigation is one of the surest ways of assuring that we shall be able to maintain that high level of production.
For example, I should like hon. members to visit the constituency of Acadia this year. The eastern part of that constituency has always been referred to as one of semipermanent drought. Yet this year for the first time since 1927 there is a very substantial crop in that district, one which will run from twenty to forty bushels to the acre. The only reason we have a crop in that area this year is that we have had a substantial amount of rainfall. This shows what might be done if irrigation were put in there.
The government has made a considerable amount of progress on these projects and I hope it will continue to proceed with them, even though the war may develop in its intensity. One other question, namely that of old age security: I have seen a number of articles in the financial press to the effect that, because we are now having to increase our defence expenditures, recommendations for the betterment of old age pensioners will have to be held in abeyance. I say the need for taking care of the old age pensioners will be that much greater, and that there is absolutely no excuse for holding in abeyance the recommendations made by the special committee to deal with old age security.
In closing let me say that in order to have an effective defence program we must proceed hand in hand with an effective program of economic development.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I first, like those who have preceded me in the debate, extend my congratulations to the mover (Mr. Cannon) and the seconder (Mr. Bennett) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. I do not intend at this time to enter into a discussion of the over-all picture of national defence, as some of the experts who have spoken before me have done. I shall leave that phase of the matter to those who are better qualified to speak with respect to it.
There are a few observations, however, I should like to make, and I make them because of talks I have had with various people in my constituency. I should like to bring their ideas and thoughts to the attention of the government and hon. members generally. Possibly if I were choosing a text to use at this time I would quote from a short article
236	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. H. O. White appearing in the Financial Times of September 1, which deals with the keynote address of the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton), and which states in part:
The keynote was sounded by defence minister Brooke Claxton when he stated that there were not many targets in the country which would appear important enough to warrant atomic attack.
That seems to me a very easy way to gloss over a serious situation. Using that as a basis for my remarks I shall pass on to some of the statements made by other speakers. The hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis) said, in effect, "Let us quit talking about unpreparedness. Let us start building our defences all along the line." I think those were his words. But that is the trouble; the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) and the Minister of National Defence claim that this has already been done. There is a difference of opinion on that point. One thing we do know is that $1,500 million has been spent, and all we have to show for it is about one brigade. The people back home are asking me, "What did you do with all that money?" They realize that they are paying, in income tax and indirect taxation of one kind or another, a very considerable sum. Partly because of that they find it difficult to buy the necessities of life-food, shelter and clothing.
May I also extend my congratulations to the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Pearkes) upon the very splendid speech he made dealing with our over-all defence picture, in which he tried to bring to the House of Commons and the people of Canada the seriousness of the situation, without at the same time attempting to make us jittery. The Minister of National Defence addressed the house in a carefully prepared speech coolly calculated to allay any fears and, if that were possible, to increase our complacency.
Let me ask this question: Did Churchill do harm to the cause in 1940 when he told the British people that he had nothing to offer but toil, sweat, blood and tears? No; he prepared them for the difficult years ahead

prepared not only the British nation but peoples throughout the world. That is quite different from the story we are told all across the board. Then, along with what we are told is the policy of hush-hush-"We dare not tell you what we are doing, for security reasons." That is just an excuse, a way out, for the government to get out from under the things they have not done, and so that they will not have to tell the people the truth.
The fact is they dare not tell the truth. Never was so little for so much-a billion and a half, and practically nothing to show for it. Some members of the government have


spoken in an abstract way. If I were asked whether I knew what they were going to do I would be at a loss to answer. I hope no one will have any doubt after I conclude as to what I mean.
The papers today tell us that our defence expenditures will be at least $625 million and probably plus that amount. I shall return again to that matter. People are asking what is being done with all this money. There is a suspicion in the minds of many people that we have built up an armchair army and will have to build up another one before we can go to Korea. I do not think the people are complaining about taxation so long as they know that the dollars are being spent in an efficient way and for the things we need. But there is considerable doubt that that is being done with the hard-earned dollars of the people.
For the last three or four sessions the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) has told us that our defences were adequate, that we were prepared and that everything was being done. Saturday Night of August 22 says, "Now a real defence". Just by a stroke of the pen by the minister we are supposed to have the real thing. I do not think anyone believes that, not even the editor of Saturday Night.
What we need is proper air defence which would provide the most modern and flexible type of defence. Our present air defence is woefully weak. An article was reprinted in the Ottawa Journal of August 5, 1950, which had appeared in Canadian Aviation and I should like to quote briefly as follows:
. . . defence minister Claxton's public assurances that we are able to repel any invasion of our territory. It is obvious to anyone with the slightest knowledge of our air power that our immediate defensive strength is pitiful.
And again:
The argument that "Eagle" was only a battalion-level exercise implied that there were significant air units elsewhere. That was not true. It is still not true today.
The aviation authorities should know what they are saying. That article has been reprinted many times and I do not think it can be denied to the satisfaction of many people in this country. We require fighter planes just as they required fighter planes at Pearl Harbor. We all recall the sneak attack that was made there and we should realize how vulnerable we are to similar attacks. After repeated assurances in the last two or three sessions that our defences were adequate we are now purchasing 100 obsolete secondhand planes.
There are three basic needs. First, air fighters; second, a mobile army to protect our

land areas; and, third a fleet to help to protect our enormous coast lines. That will be difficult but it is a problem that must be faced. Probably I should be a little more detailed as to our defence needs. In this connection I should like to refer again to the statement that there were not many strategic targets in Canada for atomic bombing. Twelve well placed bombs could do considerable damage in Ontario. Six could put our hydro power projects out of business; three could cripple our petroleum industry and three could bottle up our inland waterways.
The industrial heart of Canada would be stilled and the agricultural areas of the province would be back to the days of the horse. It would not be a question of our providing food for our allies, it would be a question of having enough food for our own people right here in Canada. Last winter in the London area there was a little local ice storm which tied up agricultural production. Most farms in Ontario are geared to hydroelectric power and we should realize how vulnerable we are in this connection. Mr. Speaker, in rising to take part in this debate, I am not going to touch on Korea. I have read a lot about Korea, and I have had quite a few conversations with the hon. member for Lambton-Kent (Mr. MacKenzie), who seems to know a good deal about the situation, having lived in that country. I learned a lot in the army. Perhaps I learned a lot of things that it would have been better for me not to learn.
Tonight I want to touch on the question of rising prices. I think what is taking place in this country at the present time is most serious. It is a tremendously big subject and covers a great amount of territory. I am sure nobody wants me to detain the house very long, and I am only going to refer to the prices of one or two articles that are annoying not only to me but to many of my constituents. I should like to deal with implement prices. In 1946 I spoke in the house about the price of farm implements at a time when the Right Hon. J. L. Ilsley, the then minister of finance, introduced a motion to increase implement dealers' prices by 12J per cent. At that time the minister had this to say, as recorded at page 894 of Hansard for April 15, 1946:
The wartime prices and trade board have satisfied themselves that 12J per cent will be sufficient to enable the companies to carry on; but they are also satisfied that, whatever the profit position may have been during the war on their war business, there is now such a drop in their profits that those profits for the ensuing year are sure to be less than average profits of the period 1936-1939.
On the same page you will find two communications, one from the Cockshutt Plow


company and the other from James S. Duncan of the Massey-Harris company. I want to read them for the benefit of the new members who did not hear them read at that time. This is what the Cockshutt Plow company had to say:
The recent increase of 121 per cent in the retail prices of farm implements is completely inadequate to cover increases in material labour and over-all costs since ceiling prices were set. While necessity for controls is appreciated such controls should be fair and equitable. Implement manufacturers should not be forced to accept staggering increases in costs without being allowed to adjust selling prices proportionately. Otherwise the industry will find itself in straitened circumstances and will be unable to carry on necessary production. The increase required by our company to provide sound operation is over 25 per cent as outlined in our submission to the wartime prices and trade board. The increase authorized by them is insufficient and will place our company in an unsound and unsatisfactory position unless augmented by a subsidy. We therefore respectfully request the matter of increases in prices of farm implements be given further consideration. Our company is in no position to manufacture implements on a losing basis.
That is what the Cockshutt Plow company had to say. I shall now read Mr. Duncan's complaint. It is as follows:
Reference recent ruling farm implement prices. Decision taken wartime prices and trade board most disappointing having in mind we submitted conclusive evidence cost advances justifying our request substantially greater percentage increase. I appreciate your difficulty and recognize that if inflationary tendencies are to be controlled that all must be prepared to make sacrifices. James S. Duncan.
From those two letters one can see that the gentlemen representing the companies were trying to prove that they would go broke if they did not get further increases. I said at that time, and I think it will be found on page 1777 of Hansard of May 22, 1946, that in 1938 the shares of the Cockshutt Plow company were quoted at $7, while the shares of the Massey-Harris company were quoted at $5.25. The day I was speaking in the house the shares had advanced to $16f for the Cockshutt company, while the shares of -the Massey-Harris company had advanced to $17J. This showed that when this application was being made there was a greater expectancy of profit than there had ever been before. From the Financial Post I find that the Cockshutt Plow company shares are now quoted at $18, and the Massey-Harris shares have advanced to $32. This indicates that both companies are in a sound financial position.

At the beginning of the forties a tractor could be purchased for approximately $1200. Today practically the same tractor costs $3000. Going back to the early forties again, a combine could be purchased for about $1,800, while today a combine sells for anywhere from $4,800 to $5,500; some of them are a little less and some are a bit more. Let us look at the net earnings of the Cockshutt Plow company. They were as follows: 1945, $266,159; 1946, $361,925; 1947, $731,439; 1948, $2,062,002; 1949, $3,070,013. This is the company that needed more than 12-J per cent to keep the business on a sound basis.
Let us look at the Massey-Harris company. The net earnings of that company were as follows: 1945, $1,588,480; 1946, $2,125,570; 1947, $4,084,067; 1948, $9,044,761; for the next eleven months only, not a complete year, the earnings were $13,367,416. If this government allows that sort of thing, then it should not be a government. It is a disgrace to permit a thing like that to continue. Every man is entitled to a fair return for his labour or a fair return on his investment, but when one finds a company making a million and a half in 1945 and making $13 million in 1949, there is something radically wrong. The Liberal party today is no longer the Liberal party of the time when I was a boy. At that time they looked after the underdog but it appears now that they are looking after the big business interests and no one else. With all the expense of labour and raw material that these companies claim to have, they are still making more money than they ever made before. I know that these companies must have profits to be successful, but it does seem to me they are taking more than they should.
Everyone maintains that the farmer is prosperous today. If the farmer is taking the opportunity of replenishing his farm machinery at today's prices, then he has not very much laid by for a rainy day. When wheat was a dollar per bushel he could buy a tractor for $1,200. Today, with wheat around $1.50 per bushel or whatever the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) will give, the farmer has to pay double the price for his tractor. So far as a combine is concerned the same thing applies, because the cost of that is up about two and a half times what it was in the early forties. When one talks about the prosperity of the farmer, one always talks about the price of beef and the high price the farmer receives for cattle. I think the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Blackmore) and the hon. member for Calgary West (Mr. Smith) talked last week about beef prices, and agreed that the farmer was
The Address-Mr. Bryce receiving about 28J cents per pound. Neither mentioned the price of feeders before they were fed.

Shortly after the Korean war broke out there arose in the press and on the air discussions as to a possible shortage of sugar.

The Address-Mr. Bryce Sugar prices were increased under the pretext that there was a shortage. At the same time, in the press and over the air, President Truman was assuring the people of this continent that there was more sugar in storage in the United States than ever before in the history of the country; and that when this was gone the sugar potential in the United States was greater than at any time in the history of the country. re-enact their price control machinery and not only to put on ceilings at the present level but to roll back those ceilings so that any increases that may have taken place since the beginning of the Korean war at least would be eliminated. I urge that action because you have that needless spiral: prices go up, the workman becomes dissatisfied, he loses his standard of living and he asks for more wages, and the thing keeps going on.
I feel strongly on this subject, and that is why I am dealing with it tonight to the exclusion of everything else. I am not thinking of workers and farmers alone, but I have particularly in mind all of those on fixed incomes: the thousands of civil servants, the old age pensioners, those on veterans' pensions, those on war veterans' allowances and the thousands on provincial mothers' allowances, blind pensions and so forth. Every increase in prices means a reduction in their standard of living, and I trust that the program recommended by the committee on social security at the last session will not be sidetracked because of the complications that have arisen in the international field. I hope that the government will go forward with that program and will as soon as possible enact the necessary legislation to relieve our aged people of the objectionable means test.
As the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) suggested, a well-organized economy internally is one of our best guarantees of meeting our international obligations.
In closing, I want to support what the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Quelch) said when he spoke of the international commodity clearing house proposal at the meeting of the FAO. We are still destroying our surpluses of food instead of diverting them to feed a hungry world. When this matter comes up for further discussion I hope the government will see its way clear to be more agreeable to such an idea or will let us know something more about it, as it would make a real contribution to world peace.

Mr. Speaker, for the few minutes I intend to speak, I am afraid I shall have to repeat some thoughts previously expressed in this debate. I feel that the importance of the matter under review requires me to state briefly to the house some views which I believe are generally held in my constituency.
The last war, in which Canada made a superhuman effort, had left us with a legitimate hope for peace among all the peoples of the world. And so, throughout the country,

Canadians were glad when an association of the free nations of the world, now known as the United Nations Organization, was established.
From the start, Canada has been a member of that organization and a signatory of the charter. As such, we assumed obligations. Among other things, we undertook to support steps providing for collective security against all aggression and to give any assistance required for the preservation of peace.
When Canada thus committed herself in 1945, we were hopeful that our country would never be called upon to carry out that undertaking, that never again would we have to come to the rescue of a democracy attacked by some horde of barbarians.
Unfortunately all the free democratic nations of the world are already asking our help in repelling an aggression conceived, backed and controlled by dictator Stalin.
Naturally all right-minded Canadians must have experienced a feeling of deep sadness when they saw that, so soon after the great war, our country was asked to carry out an undertaking given in an atmosphere of mutual trust and true peace. We had overlooked the inhuman policies of the U.S.S.R. leaders.
Again, the whole world is disturbed by war. Last June, parliament decided to send three destroyers to give assistance to the other naval units of the United Nations already involved in the Korean conflict, as well as a squadron of transport planes.
An emergency special session of parliament has now been called to approve the government's decision to recruit a special volunteer brigade 5,000 strong that will be made available to the United Nations to uphold peace and to resist Soviet aggression.
Although they are disappointed I believe the people of Canada have no alternative but to accept such a decision.
Nevertheless, there are many who regret that the United States, the country which has up to now taken the lead in resisting Soviet aggression, rejected Pandit Nehru's offer of mediation.
There could be some doubt, of course, about the-outcome of such mediation. Nevertheless, in view of the personality of the Indian leader, of the political importance of his great country, we should have given more consideration to this offer of peace from a great Asiatic leader. Unfortunately, it is too late to correct that mistake and we are now duty bound to take part in a war fought thousands of miles from our country, it -is true, but in respect of which Canada has
The Address-Mr. Balcer been called upon to do its share as a party to the United Nations charter. Even though we must train and equip that brigade for an expedition afar, and establish our national defence on a sounder basis, we should not commit ourselves to uncontrolled and exaggerated expenditures that would be prejudicial to the economy of the nation.
Canadians, naturally, want us to fulfil our obligations, but they also wish to see their money spent in a truly fair and reasonable way.
Frankly, the government has very little to show, as far as national defence is concerned, for the billion and a half dollars spent since 1945.
Those appropriations were voted by parliament, it is true, but the house could have decided more advisedly had those enormous expenditures been scrutinized by a committee of the house, as is done in Great Britain, the United States and several other countries. In my opinion, should a committee of the house be appointed, we could easily do without the blatant publicity which always follows the meetings of committees set up by our neighbours to the south.
Besides seeing to it that this money is wisely spent, I believe that the people of Canada must also know whether the government intends to limit itself to its present program or whether more surprises are in store for us.
This afternoon, the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) tried to give us some explanation of the part assigned to this country in the present conflict. In spite of his explanation, the situation still appears to me undetermined and rather hazy. Moreover, the United States, since the beginning of the Korean conflict, have, on various occasions shown signs of a fumbling policy, which was lacking in consistency and cohesion. Thus we see differences of opinions between the President of the United States and his commander-in-chief in the Far East. For instance, the army chief of staff is forced to recall one of his own generals, while the Secretary of State, Mr. Acheson, has to differ publicly with the Secretary for the Navy.
We have noted that among our neighbours to the south, the nation's policy is not clearly defined, although their soldiers continue to lay down their lives while defending a country that is a member of the United Nations against brutal soviet aggression.
242	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Balcer
I harbour grave fears that the same situation may again occur here. Of course, I wish to see our alliance with the United States continue, but I urge the government to remain ever cautious with respect to the line of action our southern neighbours would have us follow. It does not follow that, in order to meet our obligations towards the United Nations, we should accept all the decisions of the United States. We must preserve the integrity of our sovereignty for if there is one thing to which the people of my constituency are opposed, it is union with the United States.
The answer to that might be that the matter is not of current interest. However, we must not forget that our policy must be a Canadian policy supported by the whole Canadian people.
A country like ours must live up to its obligations. But I sincerely believe that with the billions of dollars that our country and the United States will be called upon to spend for armaments, our contribution to world peace would be much more effective were a peace offensive by the great Asiatic peoples which we still number among our friends to be launched simultaneously with this military action. I refer to India and Pakistan where Russian propaganda has not yet met with success. I would request the government to inaugurate a lend-lease or assistance program for those two countries. Canada has two great friends there: Pandit Nehru and Mr. Liaquat Ali Khan, whom this house had the honour of hearing. I therefore believe that Canada and the United States would make a serious mistake by not taking advantage of the support which those two great democrats can give to world peace.
It is frightening to see the United States and Canada spending billions on materials that will later be used as death-dealing weapons against the peoples of Asia.
If part of those billions that will be sunk into our intervention in Korea were only used to turn hundreds of millions of Hindus into friends filled with gratitude toward their western allies, we would be doing more for peace than by defeating aggression through armed intervention in Korea.
Moreover, because those Asiatic peoples comprise millions of human beings, nothing is to be gained by a policy of aerial bombardments and armoured tank war. The atomic 

bombs dropped by our southern allies on two Japanese cities will, in my opinion, remain as a blemish on their history.
I therefore feel, as a Christian and as a Canadian, that we should spare no efforts to promote peace and at the same time, ask our youth to enlist in order to repel the aggression of these politburo gangsters. In this struggle against the Kremlin's ideology there is no better way to gain public support than to raise the standard of living of the Asiatic democracies. We should indeed show all peoples in the world that our way of life is truly better than the soviet way and that we can extend it to all.
Let us now return to the internal situation in the face of that conflict. In addition to fighting communistic activity in Asia, the government should show the Canadian people its determination to prevent the sabotaging at home of our democracy by communists.
Ordinary common sense should make the government forget the political advantages which it may have derived as a result of its tolerant attitude towards Canadian communists, and bring it to ban their demoralizing, anti-religious and anti-social activities. Otherwise, people may easily question the government's sincerity.
The enormous expenditures resulting from our participation in the conflict will entail increased taxation. I therefore urge the government to tax first of all the large corporations instead of making individuals carry the load of taxation. Owing to the present high cost of living, I doubt very much whether it would be humanly possible for the average Canadian citizen to stand an increase in income tax.
Since the government has done nothing to curb the ever increasing cost of living it has no right to remedy the effects of its inaction by increased taxation alone. I hope it will use other methods.
Let us hope that the government will put before parliament during this session a well balanced program to fight inflation and the increasing cost of living. That is essential. If we do not want to see the recurrence of strikes such as the one which has just paralysed this country, we must tackle the problem seriously.

Finally, Mr. Speaker, I once again remind the government that our young men, while taking their place among the troops of the free nations of the world, will not be able to display any distinctive Canadian flag. They will, of course, have the United Nations flag, but in my opinion, this government will never have a better opportunity to grace this country with a truly national flag.

There are those who advocate compulsory reserve army training, but compulsory military service is not part of Canada's program. Recent figures of enlistments in the special force and the active force show that there is no need for it, at any rate at the present time. I would suggest to some members of the opposition that instead of advising young men against enlisting they should assist the recruiting of personnel for all services in every way.
All reserve units are working and training toward the day when they may be mobilized to take an active part in the defence of this country. Too many people believe that the reserve army is nothing more or less than a social club. In our own unit, when it is indicated clearly that an individual cannot or will not attend training, prompt action is taken to collect his kit and strike him off strength, and this applies equally to officers, W.O.'s, N.C.O.'s and men.
We feel that present conditions require a definite change in attitude toward administration and training on the part of all ranks, and this would include the C.O. and the last joined trooper. We must all walk a little faster and accomplish more than has been the case in the peacetime soldiering of the past. The N.P.A.M., which was the reserve army between wars, gave a good account of itself during world war II. Today's reserve army is better prepared than its earlier counterpart to render a like service.
In conclusion I should like to add that in the struggle today between two ways of life arms alone are not enough. There is a need for us to help in an economic way the peoples who are now wondering which way to turn. We may have time for this before they need military aid or it may be necessary for us to help them economically at the same time as we help them to strengthen their defences. Even this is not enough. In order to offset the propaganda which is emanating from the Kremlin it is necessary that we inform the undecided peoples of our objective in this world struggle,' not so much a resistance of communism as a championing of the cause of economic and political freedom.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, although the speech from the throne at the opening of this session departs from


the usual practice of dealing with many subjects I feel I am justified in following the time-honoured custom of congratulating the mover (Mr. Cannon) and the seconder (Mr. Bennett) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. I should like especially to congratulate the mover upon his wonderful facility of speech in both languages as well as upon the contents of his speech.
On Saturday afternoon the Independent hon. member for Beauce (Mr. Poulin) when discussing the vital questions before us advocated a purely defensive policy on the part of Canada and opposed the sending of any assistance to resist aggression in southern Korea. At the time the hon. member was speaking there were probably hundreds of thousands of people in Ontario and Quebec listening to the broadcasts of two battles that were taking place, one at Lansdowne Park in Ottawa and one at the Stadium in Montreal. One can imagine the consternation or pleasure that was shown by the supporters of the Alouettes or the Rough Riders or the Argos as fortune favoured one side or the other.
But at the same time in the southeast corner of far off Korea there were battle-stained and weary and outnumbered United Nations troops, southern Koreans and members of the United States forces on the ten-yard line struggling their best to hold it against the ferocious North Koreans who were backed by the might of Soviet Russia. It seemed to me that if there could have been a broadcast of what was taking place in South Korea on Saturday afternoon there would have been greater urgency on the part of all hon. members, and especially on the part of members of the government, to send help to that beleaguered little country.
During the past week we have had interesting speeches by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson), by the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) and by the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent). While I did not have the pleasure of hearing the Prime Minister's speech I did follow with close interest the remarks of the other two ministers. I always have great pleasure in following the graceful speeches of the Secretary of State for External Affairs but I think on the last occasion the Minister of National Defence almost outdid him.
Yet I think if we could have listened to a couple of South Koreans, through an interpreter of course, or to a couple of United States G.I.'s, giving us in their blunt language an account of what was happening in their area when the North Koreans punched a hole eight miles deep on the western flank of that 120-mile front, there would not have been much difficulty about getting help to South

Korea. The Secretary of State for External Affairs seems to be surprised that there should be any demand from this side of the house that help should have been sent to that country.
Canada today is a great nation. At other sessions of this parliament we have been often told about how great she was. That seems to have been soft-pedalled at the present time. We are not now being told about how prosperous she is, about how great her trade is, about the soundness of her financial policies. Yet, because of her great wealth, because of her prosperity, because of the excellent manner in which she conducted her financial, military and naval affairs during the past war, and particularly the exploits of her air force, Canada acquired a reputation and prestige in the world far beyond what she would have been entitled to on the basis of her population alone. Because of that and because she is a permanent member of the United Nations, because she faces the Pacific as well as the Atlantic, Canada has an interest in what is going on in eastern Asia second only to that of the United States.
During the past week there was distributed a white paper dealing with Canada and the Korean crisis and which gives the details of the appeal contained in the telegram sent by the Secretary General of the United Nations to the acting Canadian permanent delegate to the United Nations under date of July 14. This reads:
In this connection I have been advised that there is an urgent need for additional effective assistance. I should be grateful, therefore, if your government would examine its capacity to provide an increased volume of combat forces, particularly ground forces.
On July 19 the Prime Minister made a statement in which he said:
Having in mind the other obligations for the employment of Canadian ground forces, the cabinet has reached the conclusion that the dispatch, at this stage, of existing first line elements of the Canadian army to the Korean theatre would not be warranted.
The acting permanent delegate wrote on July 21:
With respect to ground forces, for the reasons indicated in a statement issued by the Prime Minister on 19 July (of which I am enclosing a copy) the Canadian government is unable, at this stage, to dispatch existing first line elements of the Canadian army to the Korean theatre.
We appreciate a reasonable explanation, Mr. Speaker, of why the Canadian government is not sending ground forces to help in Korea, but this afternoon, when we were listening to the Secretary of State for External Affairs, he commented on a remark made by the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Pearkes) on Saturday, and said that there was no appeal from General MacArthur. I think I
The Address-Mr. W. J. Browne am quoting him correctly when I say that he said an appeal had not come from General MacArthur. In today's Ottawa Citizen there is an account from Lake Success of a third appeal from General MacArthur. It reads:
General Douglas MacArthur pleaded Saturday for a quick build-up of United Nations ground forces in Korea. He said in a report to the United Nations that naval and air power have grown in strength and effectiveness but added: "My gravest concern is for a prompt build-up of the now outnumbered ground forces of this command. ... I still feel it my duty to report to you that contributions must be forthcoming without delay if this threat to international security is to be resolved promptly."
This report is his third. Is it not tragic that when this repeated call came Canada was unprepared to give any assistance? The criticism directed at the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) and other members of the government is not so much that they did not wish to send troops as that they were not in a position to send troops at all because they did not have them to send. My colleague, the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. Higgins), has pointed out that if Norway were attacked Canada would have no troops to send there under the Atlantic charter, or if Newfoundland had been attacked Canada would have had no troops to send there. It is because they have neglected their duty that people are criticizing them today.
In this house I have the honour to represent a riding composed of the three provincial districts of Ferryland, Placentia-St. Mary's and St. John's West. In the referenda which were held to decide the question of confederation those three districts gave the largest majority against union with Canada. Nevertheless, when I was home this summer, I consulted many of the residents of this riding and asked them two questions. I said, "What do you think of the war?" and "Do you think that Canada is doing all it should?" The answers I received were invariably these: "We think the war is very serious and we do not think Canada is doing enough". When these people told me that, I believe their views represented what the people in other parts of Canada are saying and thinking today. The Secretary of State for External Affairs has, I believe, a large and talented staff under his command. He has control of diplomats, ministers and charges d'affaires in about forty foreign countries. In addition to these, he also has representatives under his direction at the United Nations. Canada even had a Canadian representative on the United Nations commission on Korea who was responsible indirectly at least to the Secretary of State for External Affairs. From these people he could get the latest information about what was transpiring

The Address-Mr. W. J. Browne in the world. Although the Secretary of State for External Affairs shakes his head in negative fashion, I think he ought to be the best informed man in this house.

speechtext:
In January and February of this year a debate took place in Washington on this very question of aid to the Far East and Korea. I do not know whether the minister has seen the report of that debate, but certainly when he returned from his trip to the Far East and spoke in the house on February 22, although he devoted two or three pages of his account to his meeting with General MacArthur, he made no reference to this very important debate that had taken place in the house of representatives at Washington. I should like to quote from a summary of the congressional proceedings of the United States for January to April inclusive, 1950. I may say that a bill was introduced to give aid to southern Korea and when it was first introduced it was defeated by one vote. It was introduced again at the instance of Senator Connally and was passed by a large majority. I want to draw the attention of the house to what was said during that debate by two Republican representatives, although the measure was Democratic in origin. At page 57 I find the following:
Hon. William Lemke, Republican, said ... as a member of a visiting subcommittee he had been in Hong Kong and Korea. At Tokyo they had been informed by General MacArthur's staff of the danger of world war III and there was no use camouflaging the danger. The member felt that "we owe some obligation to the Korean people that we put in the position they are in, and also to realize that our war is in Asia, not in Europe." They had been shown in General MacArthur's headquarters that the division of Korea was very unfortunate and dangerous to America. "We were informed in no uncertain terms that Russia was supplying arms and training North Korea, and we

were . . . doing the same for South Korea. That is the situation that exists there today." The South Koreans could take care of themselves unless Russia stepped in. When she did, then world war III was on, and they need not camouflage it.
The remarks of the Hon. Charles A. Eaton are summarized as follows:
U.S. policy in the Orient had been a most disastrous one in recent years, in his opinion; and he looked on this little group in the peninsula of Korea as the last toehold the U.S. had on the Asiatic continent at the present moment. The Koreans were worthy people; they had a great history. The shadow of Russia hung over them all the time. Because America was now face to face with a world challenge, which sooner or later would have to be decided by a terrific sacrifice of men and treasure, the member did not want to see South Korea at this moment withdraw from the one spot in all of dark Asia where people were struggling to be free and had a right to expect American assistance.
I notice that sitting with the Secretary of State for External Affairs is the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Mayhew), who accompanied him on his trip to Colombo, and I believe visited Tokyo with him on his return journey. I believe the two ministers were in Tokyo after that debate had taken place. They were in a position to be fully informed about what was going on in Korea, but when the minister spoke to the house he gave us no information and at no time indicated how serious the situation was there.
In view of the importance of that debate that took place in the house of representatives, I cannot understand why the government refused the reasonable request that was made by the men of military experience on this side of the house when they requested that a committee be set up to examine into the defence estimates. These estimates were presented in large blocks, and it was impossible for any member to analyse them. Why was it that the government would not agree to setting up that committee for an examination of those expenditures to see if the country was getting value for the hundreds of millions of dollars that were expended? Last spring we voted about $400 million, and made commitments for another $200 million over the next two years. It seems to me that the government had a good reason for refusing a committee. They did not want to have witnesses brought here to show how the defence department was frittering away the people's money.
If the statement made here by the hon. member for Calgary East (Mr. Harkness) is correct, and it has not been denied, that Canada was not in a position to send any more than one battalion, then I say the minister should hang his head in shame and the government deserves the most severe condemnation by the people of this country. The Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. SEPTEMBER 4, 1950
Pearson) made some reference to the part that he thought Germany should play in a joint defence of western Europe. I was glad to hear the minister make those remarks. I made similar remarks about a year ago, although I do not profess to have any special knowledge of international affairs. Is it not common sense? Ten or twelve years ago Germany was one of the greatest military powers, and today in western Germany there are millions of trained soldiers. We are permitting them to watch the events that are taking place, but we have not done anything up to the present time to get them to assist us in defending western culture against the barbaric menace that threatens us through Soviet Russia. In the United Nations meetings at Lake Success and elsewhere insulting words are hurled across the table by the Russians and to the Russians. Although we realize how powerful Russia has become since 1945, we have not taken the measures we should have taken to arm the people of western Germany, and to make them valiant allies in our defence. It is good news that the present chancellor of Germany does not wish to have Germany armed as an independent power, but rather wishes her to be associated with the other western European countries in the defence of western Europe and what we hold dear. It is a good thing that General Charles de Gaulle, that brilliant tank expert of world war II, has said that the future of the world depends to a large extent on the association of Germany and France.
The world owes a debt of gratitude, Mr. Speaker, to the United States; not only for the tremendous amount of money that country has forwarded to Europe for its rehabilitation, but for the military protection it has given to enable us to continue our march of prosperity and extend our social security. Everyone seems to leave everything to Uncle Sam. It hardly seems fair. We are not playing our full part as an ally when we leave it all up to the United States. .

It was not
wise for Canada to allow her defences to fall into disrepair or to be dissipated on the auction block.
There is another subject, Mr. Speaker, to which the member for Calgary East referred, and that is the question of Spain. I have referred to Spain before. The people of Newfoundland, as well as the people in other parts of Canada, are wondering why it is that the Canadian government is so particular about its dealings with Spain. Why are the
The Address-Mr. W. J. Browne governments of other countries so fussy about exchanging diplomatic representation with Spain when they do so with Yugoslavia? According to reports, conditions in Yugoslavia are not much superior to those which we believe exist in Soviet Russia. General Franco, known as the dictator of Spain, shares with Chiang Kai-shek the honour of being Russia's number one enemy. Russia has never forgiven Chiang Kai-shek for preventing China from falling into the hands of the communists many years ago. When I hear people criticizing Chiang Kai-shek and talking of throwing him to the wolves, I think they are forgetting the good government he gave China for many years. We have not been subjected to the same infiltration of communism that China experienced. Some hon. members here must remember that while Chiang Kai-shek was in power in China the missionaries from this and other countries could carry on their work of spreading Christianity without any fear of interference from the government. Conditions are far different today; yet some people are anxious to see the government that is in power in China today receive recognition while Chiang Kai-shek, who fought so stubbornly against the Japanese and who was our ally for so many years, should now be discarded. It is a strange commentary upon the loyalty of men that first of all Poland and then Chiang Kai-shek-I suppose there are others-should be discarded in this fashion.
When the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) was speaking this afternoon he suddenly reminded us we should not put too much confidence in armed forces. He said it in such a solemn tone of voice that, for a moment, I thought he was going to refer to the spiritual forces upon which we should rely. Instead of that he surprised a good many when he said that we have our scientists to depend upon. I think, Mr. Speaker, that it is not inappropriate in this house, which begins its session with daily prayer, that we should feel we are all in God's hands at this moment. Nobody knows what is going to take place in the world. We are entirely dependent upon Almighty God. We ought to look to Him, trust in Him, and ask Him to help us to do what is right in this tragic situation.
In the Roman Catholic church this is a holy year. Millions of people have gone to Rome from various parts of the world to see and hear the Holy Father, who has been ceaselessly pleading for a proper peace with justice. I think, Mr. Speaker, that we in this house, and in this country, would have greater success if we put more of our dependence upon a spiritual appeal to Almighty God than

The Address-Mr. W. J. Browne we do in reliance upon material things. Too great reliance upon material things has lulled our people into apathy and ignorance. They are told that all is well and they concentrate on getting richer and forget more vital needs.
What is the situation in the world today? We are confronted with a soviet government which is militaristic in its attitude, imperialistic in its policy, materialistic in its way of life and its philosophy, and atheistic in its religion. It is entirely opposed to everything that Christian people hold dear; and although we do not carry out fully the Christian gospel, fundamentally the people in the western countries of Europe and of America are Christian in their outlook.
There is no doubt of the aims of Soviet Russia. They are published in every book written by Russians. There is no doubt of the means Russia is willing to employ to achieve those aims. Their aim is world domination of the lives and souls of men, nothing less. The government of Russia today is as cruel and as ruthless as the government of nazi Germany ever was. It wishes, like a great spider, to have all the nations of the world enmeshed in the web it has been weaving for us; and Stalin sits like a great spider in the centre of that web and watches the nations of the world carrying on in a gay, frivolous or careless manner, neglectful of their vital needs.
In all the lands of the world the agents of Stalin are penetrating into the most secret places. They have been sitting in this chamber. They have penetrated into the greatest governments of the world and have secured secrets which have been sent from Washington to Moscow to be used for our overthrow and our enslavement.
During the past week, Mr. Speaker, the world witnessed two anniversaries, but I have heard no reference in this house to those two important events. On September 1 we witnessed the eleventh anniversary of the invasion of Poland by Germany; and on September 2 we witnessed the anniversary of the surrender of Japan to the United States in 1945. In those six years that passed between 1939 and 1945 surely the world had its full measure of blood, sweat and tears. Poland, which was invaded then, our gallant ally, is an enemy now. Does anyone ever stop to inquire how it came about that Poland is now regarded as an enemy, when we know that 90 per cent of the people of that country are not inimical to western civilization? Or why Japan, which was a defeated enemy in 1945, should today be regarded as a potential ally? In that country, as in Germany, there are 80 millions of people and several


millions of trained, able and skilful soldiers who could be used, if the need arose, to resist Soviet aggression.
At the same time the might of the Soviet union has grown. Did Russia neglect her defences as Canada did? Did she disperse her armies? Not according to the most reliable information we can get or according to the movies in which we sometimes see Stalin reviewing the troops in the Red square in Moscow, and see tanks in their thousands; armoured cars and guns; and young, tough, well-armed troops in their hundreds of thousands. Where are Canada's guns, her armoured cars, her tanks and her troops? Since I came to Canada a year ago I have not seen a tank or an armoured car; and the only parade of troops that I have seen has been at the piling of the drums or at the opening of parliament out here on parliament hill.
All these are extremely serious matters, and I would ask hon. members not to be frivolous about them. They will have a different attitude in a short time. I do not know what is going to happen, and they do not know any more than I do. What I am pointing out are facts. When we hear from the masters of schooners and the captain of the steamer that crosses the straits between North Sydney and Port aux Basques that submarines are around our coast; when the captain says that one was within fifty yards away from the S.S. Cabot Strait as he went across; when we see reports in the papers that submarines are reported off Australia and off Japan; and when we are informed on the highest authority that those are Russian submarines, it is time for us to take the smile off our faces and look at things realistically.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, I ask the question that the President of the United States asked: What is the state of this nation? What is the state of Canada at the present time? The empty skies, the silent seas give us our answer. It is regrettable that Canada has neglected her defences. But it is some consolation to know that at last the government is listening and has wakened up to the real state of affairs. Let us hope it has been in time.

Mr. Speaker, in the remarks that will follow I intend to express personal opinions which are familiar to the electors of the constituency I represent. I have listened with a great deal of attention to the speech from the throne and the statement of the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) on the amounts we

shall be asked to vote as war appropriations. This is not the first time an increase in appropriations tor military purposes has been mentioned. I doubt very much, however, that these colossal amounts are devoted only to the defence of our country. A past, too recent to be forgotten, leads us to doubt it. I can recall the years 1937-1938 when, as September 1939 drew closer, appropriations for so-called national defence were increasing. We have paid dearly to learn that these appropriations served to draw us into a war in which Canada had never been attacked.
In 1939, Canada threw herself into the war two years before the United States. We gained nothing. We have good reason to be worried. A storm, perhaps unprecedented, is gathering on the international horizon. Wars on the foreign front have been prepared with so-called defence armaments.
Great Britain and the United States have war departments, while in Canada, perhaps through euphemism or in order to hide the true purpose of that department, we call it Department of National Defence. It might be that we want to give the impression that Canada does not intend to attack any other nation. Yet we have, on two occasions, fought wars waged several thousand miles from our shores, although no one had attacked us. Where will those so-called national defence budgets take us now?
Following the cataclysm of 1914-18, I heard representatives of this country thunder against those who had dragged us into that mess. It was considered as a sort of crime. We even fostered an attitude of non-belligerency, especially in the province of Quebec. Those who had decried the scourge of war did worse.
I well remember the speech made in this house on May 24, 1938 by Mr. William Lyon Mackenzie King. I quote from page 3178 of Hansard:
We know and the world knows that we have neither the power nor the will to attack any other land for our own ends. Nor are we inclined to organize or join in crusades in other continents . . . We have neither the power nor the knowledge to settle the destinies of countries thousands of miles away. We are no more likely of our own motion to intervene in Europe than Sweden or Bulgaria or Switzerland is to intervene in America.
Let us now see what the Hon. Ernest Lapointe, former minister of justice and father of the present Minister of Veterans Affairs, had to say at Quebec on December 13, 1938. I quote:
Instead of waging war in foreign lands, we shall stay here and defend our beloved Canada.
Speaking at St. Henri, Mr. P. J. A. Cardin, former minister of public works, went even
The Address-Mr. Courtemanche farther, as reported by Le Canada of January 17, 1938. I quote:
This is the tenth time I am asserting it, Canada will not participate in any external war. This is the tenth time the Right Hon. W. L. Mackenzie King has repeated it before the Canadian parliament. He said it first of all in Geneva before the whole world and Britain's representatives, when he stated that Canada would have no part in any war outside her own territory. What else do you expect? Could you think of anything better . . . You have the statements of cabinet ministers and the prime minister himself ... the military appropriations of the government are earmarked simply and solely for the defence of Canada ... I am personally committed against extra-territorial participation . . .
And Mr. Cardin added in conclusion:
I am 100 per cent for the defence of my country.
I would be 150 per cent for it if that was at all possible: but when other nations are at war, don't count on me.
Those are unequivocal statements, but we have been thrown just the same into foreign wars. We have thousands of dead to bear testimony.
As regards the matter with which we are dealing, what position should we take with respect to Korea? Along with Dr. Gordon Rothney, professor of history at Sir George Williams College, who expressed this opinion at a lecture delivered on July 13, 1950, before the Montreal West Rotary Club, I answer:
Canada is the country that would suffer the most from a third world war. We must adopt an essentially Canadian policy and we must not intervene in Korea.
If the United States, for considerations that I need not discuss, have chosen to rush headlong into an affair the nature of which they know nothing about, Canada should not follow them. At the risk of being called a communist or a fellow traveller, I will add that we must not send expeditionary forces outside the country, since past experience has shown that they lead directly to conscription. Mobilization for service abroad inevitably leads to conscription as soon as the need for it is felt. We must avoid becoming involved1 in conflicts that arise between great powers and restrict our part to that of mediator.
In the light of the facts and in view of the statements made by Liberal leaders during the last thirty years, I cannot approve the stand taken, by the government in the Korean war. Bureaucrats are already rejoicing over the United States intervention in Korea in the hope that it will be followed by a third world war and that their power will be restored. Our intervention means the ration system and controls of all kinds in the near future. Our economy will again be disrupted
150	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Courtemanche and there is cause to wonder whether this time Canada will recover from all those unpropitious ventures.
Liberal propagandists are already hard at work; they even go so far as to quote certain excerpts from "O Canada", which this government refuses to recognize as our national anthem, such as: "You were born from a proud race" in order to draw all the more easily an assent which the right thinking majority of this country does not and never will want to give.
Yes, we were born from proud races and we shall never forget that we have been betrayed. Sons of proud races, we shall remember that some of our purest and noblest blood flowed uselessly on foreign soil during two wars which were to have put an end to other wars, including this one.
Aware that I am voicing the will of the majority of my people, I believe it is my duty to rise against Canada's participation in this war where co-nationals are destroying one another. Let us not hurl our country into another disaster.
My stand should astonish no one. I represent my electors in this house and they will never approve a position which apparently must lead my country, our country, to final disaster.
How can we logically explain the about-face of the newspaper Le Canada since July 5, 1950? Yet that newspaper is known to represent truest Liberal opinion in the province of Quebec. I quote an editorial from the July 5, 1950, issue entitled, "North Korea wanted friendly unification":
It Is interesting to note that ten days before launching its surprise attack. North Korea had invited Seoul authorities and members of the UNO commission in Korea for the purpose of a peaceful unification of the country.
Nothing was done, however. After dealing with strongly sovietized North Korea, the newspaper says of South Korea:
-where the former nationalist leader Syngman Rhee, with United States backing, had established a dictatorial regime that has grown increasingly unpopular. Washington had even warned president Syngman Rhee that credits to South Korea would be suspended if he did not act in a more democratic manner, and did not straighten the country's finances.
On July 7, 1950, the same newspaper denounces the political elements who in this country-
-promptly take advantage of such events to ask that the nation be put on a useless and ruinous war footing.
On July 11, 1950, an editorial warned against what might lead to another war.
IMr. Courtemanche.]

On July 13, 1950, a radical change occurs. Under the title: "Our destroyers will serve the cause of peace," an editorial states:
By intervening today in Korea, the Canadian navy is helping to save Canada from a war of aggression in the future.
On July 25, 1950, another editorial praises Canadian and United States intervention in Korea. Later on, the policy remains the same. Those who do not support the government's intervention in Korea are communists or fellow-travellers.
All those statements convince me more than ever that we should not take part in that conflict, for the following reasons:
After taking part in two world wars, Canada cannot afford to participate in a third. The first two already cost Canada too much in both men and money. The war of 1914-18 cost us $1,225 million and that of 1939-1945, $15,130 million. Between 1939 and 1945 one million Canadians were called to arms. Is that not too much for us?
People will say that we must heed the threat of communism. Let us start by fighting it in Canada, for we are not doing so. Why should we intervene in Korea when we refrained from doing so elsewhere? It is not the first Soviet conquest. When Estonians, Latvians, Lithuanians, Poles, Germans, Austrians, Hungarians, Bulgarians, Roumanians, Chinese and others were victims of Russian terror and communist oppression, we stood idly by. Why should Korea be considered more important than other countries?
In Canada, we are still refusing to ban communism. Moscow's emissaries are permitted to travel at will, their propaganda is broadcast by His Majesty's radio stations and, if necessary, during electoral campaigns, the Liberals do not shy at communist support. One has only to remember the Grey North byelection! Shall we, all in the same breath, spend enormous sums of money and shed the blood of our Canadians to fight communism abroad, when we have not the gumption to destroy it at home? That does not make sense.
Nothing in the history of the Korean conflict justifies our intervention.
Indeed, after following in the wake of London in the past, we are now tied to Washington's apron strings. We want to play the part of a great nation, of a great power; we do not have the means to do it, nor any interest at stake.
Are the lessons of the past so soon forgotten? Did not the great powers show

The Address-Mr. Adamson
towards us a most revolting ingratitude? For once, let us think of ourselves.
Even if the French Canadian members of the Liberal party are silent and thus favour intervention, my words express the general opinion of the French Canadian people.
