That need not surprise anyone; we are Canadians first and foremost, and our desire for peace was fostered in us especially by the Liberals who have always told us that it was best to vote for them in order to avoid conscription and participation in foreign wars. The Liberals, who ceaselessly raised the spectre of conscription in the province of Quebec, were quick to adopt it later when they seemed to derive pleasure from forcing us to take part in foreign conflicts.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, may I be permitted to read an article which Pamfll Saicaru, former representative in the Roumanian parliament, has written in his book "Nothing but Ashes":
In the foreseeable future, open warfare between Russia and the United States appears as unthinkable as a fight between an elephant and a whale.
We have since learned that Soviet Russia does not live up to her commitments. That belated discovery is in no way a credit to the political acumen of Europe and the United States. It only serves to stress the shallow and irresponsible way in which have been tackled the problems raised by the war and the historical prospects of the expansion of Russian imperialism in its new form.
Should Canada pay for that lack of foresight? Let us stay out of this conflict. Let us have enough courage to fight communism at home, to begin with. We are told that this nation is too young to have its own flag. We must then be also too young to take part in this struggle, which may well develop into the bloodiest that the world has ever witnessed.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I regret very much that I cannot agree with the statements which have just been made, no matter how sincerely the hon. member has felt them.
In rising to take part in the debate on the Korean situation, I do so at probably the darkest point in the whole history of the campaign. The late news has just announced that the communists have made a further penetration of some sixteen and a half miles on one front and twelve miles on another. But, Mr. Speaker, there is a more ominous note in the tone of the dispatches. During the war we were conditioned by certain phrases used in broadcasts to denote coming reverses. I may say that the ominous note in the broadcasts and dispatches we have recently had from the United Nations, and over the air from Korea, seems to me to be preparing us for a possible evacuation. I hope events of the next few days will prove that I am wrong; but that is the inescapable situation which faces us this night.
Between the end of the last session and the beginning of this one a very able empire statesman in the person of the Prime Minister of Australia visited Ottawa. He made a speech, which I very much regret he could not make to the House of Commons in session, in which he laid down three cardinal points for any democratic government at the present time. They were, first, to be prepared to fight for our freedom; second, to continue to expand our economy and improve our society; and, third, to prevent inflation from destroying us. This program entails hard work, greater production and the placing of national duty before individual rights and pleasures. It is not the sort of platform for a political party to go to the country on, but unless we endorse it we shall not have

The Address-Mr. Adamson political parties in Canada or the right to express political opinions. Political life today is not a popularity contest.
We talk a lot about our preparations for war and in the next day or two no doubt we shall be talking about our increased expenditures and the consequent tax burden which will have to be imposed. Let us compare our efforts in the past with the efforts of the other nations of what I shall call the Atlantic community. The figures which I shall give come from the Bank for International Settlements and express the percentage of national income spent on defence before Korea. The figures are as follows:
Per Cent
United Kingdom	7-4
Netherlands	61
United States	5-9
Turkey	5-8
France	50
Italy	3-8
Sweden	3-6
Canada	30
Switzerland	2-7
Belgium	2-5
Canada is quite low on the list, being almost in last place. After Korea, the United States and United Kingdom spending on defence will approximate ten per cent of their national income. Were we to contemplate the expenditure on defence of ten per cent of our national income it would mean an expenditure of between $1,000 million and $1,500 million per year. Those are sobering figures, yet they are what the nationals of our partners in the preservation of freedom are spending. Before we speak too boastfully of our efforts let us remember what our partners are doing.
I should like to quote three paragraphs of an article which appeared in the London Economist of recent date, I think of August 1, as follows:
For all practical purposes it is true to say that the British defence effort, which ever since the end of the war has been the highest, relative to the national resources, of any of the free nations, will stand comparison as measured by expenditure, even with the newly proposed scale of American preparations.
Where the principle of equal sacrifice requires much greater efforts is among those members of the Atlantic community other than the United States and the United Kingdom.
That everybody deplores the tragic need for heavier spending on armaments ought to go entirely without saying. But if any of the free nations are tempted to argue that they cannot afford to spend more, they might be reminded that the Soviet union, a much poorer country per head, manages according to Mr. Shinwell to spend at least 13 (and I have heard the figure put at 17 by other well informed people) per cent of its national income on armaments. If there is anything the free nations cannot afford, it is that their response shall fall dangerously short of the challenge.

At the turn of the century, when referring to Canada, Kipling had this to say in his poem entitled, "Our Lady of the Snows":
Daughter am I in my mother's house,
But mistress in my own.
The word "mistress" has two meanings. One is as Kipling used it and the other is to describe a kept woman. Unless we are prepared to play our part equally with the other nations of the Atlantic community the other appellation for mistress may apply to our country. A kept woman is a role which does not fit the heroic and adventurous character of the Canadian people.
The bad publicity we have received both here and in New York has been due to many factors. There is an article which appeared in a recent issue of Maclean's magazine by Blair Fraser, who cannot be considered to be anything but friendly to the present administration. Speaking of the United States reaction to our behaviour since the outbreak of the Korean war, he says:
Mike Pearson, in a speech the night of Trygve Lie's appeal, said Canada's contribution of three destroyers was "no mere token". He meant it too. If one of those destroyers should be sunk Canadian loss of life would be more than all Americans killed in the first month of hostilities. However, the remark got a sour response in Washington. One state department man said, "O.K., let's call it three tokens." The wisecrack was picked up immediately and might be called the unofficial United States reaction to the Pearson statement.
The public relations of the Canadian army have been extraordinarily inept. At the time of the Korean crisis they publicized an exercise of one officer and ten other ranks testing gear in the Arctic. They dubbed the exercise "Exercise Shoofly". The press release said that army officers felt that the exercise had been aptly named. Things of this sort are first of all bad national defence. Second, they are extraordinarily bad publicity at a time when the free world must stick together. It has been said, "What is the good of sending our ground forces to Korea?" I wonder whether General Mac-Arthur would have welcomed even one battalion of Canadian troops even if he had to supply them through United States supply lines.
This afternoon the Secretary of State for External Affairs made an extraordinary statement. He said that no action could have been taken by the United Nations if it had not been for the fortuitous absence of the Soviet delegate from the security council when the decision was made. Does that mean that if the Soviet delegate had been present at the meeting and had vetoed the United Nations action we and the rest of the free

world would have had to sit idly by, take no action, and let the North Korean communists invade South Korea? If it does I suggest that an immediate revision of the responsibilities of the Atlantic pact nations be undertaken to overcome that difficulty.
Much has been said about our actions in the meetings of the United Nations. We are the most democratic people in the world when it comes to talking. We can talk a better Utopia than almost any other of the United Nations. But when it comes to action, as the old song goes, we simply fade away. I refer to the sort of things that have gone on in the United Nations, the sort of things thcjt the press and radio of Canada have said were wonderful things that we did. For instance, there was the genocide resolution. If there is a third world war, of what use is a pious genocide resolution when fully a third of the world's population is likely to be destroyed?
There was another instance when Mr. Ilsley.went down to the United Nations, and in a wrangle came out with the phrase that Canada was a peacemonger. The press and the radio played it up as if it were the second coming of the Messiah and said what a wonderful thing this suggestion of peace-mongering was. Such talk, Mr. Speaker, is not realistic, and does more to destroy the effectiveness of the United Nations than anything I can think of. When the actual slaughter begins we are fine. In fact Canada's slaughtering powers are as good as or better than anybody else's. If the civilian population could know what nice quiet Canadian boys can do when roused they would be surprised. Probably it is as well that they do not know.
Where we fall down is between the last part of the talking period and the beginning of the slaughtering period. This is unfortunately a political legacy which is now costing us dearly in prestige, and may result in loss of life unnecessarily as did the shocking reinforcement policy of the last war. As an example, there is our withdrawal from the duty imposed on the United States, Great Britain and France of providing at least in small measure a part of the occupying forces in Germany. This was symptomatic of the policy followed by the Liberal administration for the last quarter of a century which can be summed up in two words, no commitments. If we had undertaken a part of that job we would now have trained men and officers who would know the conditions, topography and the possible places where war in Europe might take place.
The Address-Mr. Adamson
We would also have a fund of military intelligence which is only possible through an occupying force. We are, Mr. Speaker, politically frightened at preparedness. Korea is our last chance to prevent a third world war. If we, the free people, are driven out of Korea a third world war will follow whenever and wherever Russia chooses. Korea is relatively as important, and represents about the same stage, as the occupation of the Rhineland and the breaking of the Locarno pact by Hitler. Had we stopped Hitler at that time it might have been possible-it probably would have been possible [DOT]-to prevent a second world war. Once we allowed the forces of nazism to get away with a flagrant breach of that treaty, they could get away with anything. So it is, Mr. Speaker, in Korea. If we allow the Russians-and it is the Russians because communism knows no national boundaries-to get away with the occupation of Korea the third world war is upon us. Korea is our last chance.
I do not want to go into it in detail, but I wish hon. members would read General Mac-Arthur's report to the United Nations published in yesterday's New York Times. In three places he implores them to send ground troops. He says that the American forces are outnumbered three, four, and sometimes even seven to one. In the last part of the dispatch he says:
My greatest concern is for the prompt build-up of the now outnumbered ground forces of the command.
The sands of time of our freedom are running out.
I want to speak briefly on the question of a defence committee. The Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) is fortunate in that he has an efficient committee, which not only considers his estimates but has his experts before the members of the committee. The members of that committee are informed on the problems met by Canada abroad. It has been said that since the set-up of that committee the Canadian House of Commons has become one of the best informed elective assemblies on the question of international affairs; that is what that committee has done. There have been no witch hunts. Many years ago one can remember in this house and elsewhere statements like this, "What do we need all those embassies for; why do we need these palatial buildings in Paris, Rome and Washington?" One does not hear that remark now, Mr. Speaker, because the committee of this house has gradually been able to inform the members as to the reasons for our embassies and diplomats.

The Address-Mr. Adamson The other night the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) made a statement in which he referred to what I can only call the maverick behaviour of one Senator McCarthy in the United States. His behaviour is now being called "ordeal by slander" by many of the state department officials, particularly Mr. Lattimore. Now, Mr. Speaker, to suggest that members of this house would behave in that manner does not, I think, do the Prime Minister justice.
It being eleven o'clock, Mr. Speaker, may I move the adjournment of the debate?
Motion agreed to and debate adjourned.
Mr. Speaker, may we know what the business will be tomorrow?
